speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister whether he can give the house any information arising out of his discussions with the President of the United States in respect of whether any agreement has been reached between United States and Canada as to the position they will take vis-avis the situation in the Middle East, and particularly with reference to the right of access of the state of Israel and all other nations to the gulf of Aqaba?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-STATEMENT FOLLOWING DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed to deal with that question as best I can, within the limitations of the fact that our conversations yesterday were of course confidential, as they were bound to be in the circumstances.
I do not think, however, I am betraying any confidence when I say there was complete agreement between the president and myself as to the special importance of two
602	COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry things in connection with the Middle East crisis. The first was the importance of maintaining the right of access to and innocent passage through the gulf of Aqaba, and that everything possible should be done through the United Nations to see if this can be arranged so that this danger spot can be removed.
The other danger spot, if I may call it that, about which we talked and where we agreed on certain ideas as a means of helping to remove the danger, is in the confrontation of the two forces on the Israeli-U.A.R. border, and the grave and great importance of placing on that border a United Nations presence. This would not be the United Nations Emergency Force, which has been disbanded, but in some appropriate way there must be a United Nations presence there which Will operate on both sides of the border.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-STATEMENT FOLLOWING DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Was there any discussion of the proposal of General de Gaulle, the President of the French republic, with reference to the possibility of a meeting of the four great powers to see whether within the framework of the United Nations these powers might agree on some course of action which would prevent the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-STATEMENT FOLLOWING DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter was discussed at some length. It was felt that as the question is now before the Security Council nothing should be done to weaken its position in this connection, and that a meeting of the permanent members of that body-the four powers that have been mentioned -within the context of the Security Council might be a very useful procedure at this time.
My own view, as I expressed it, was that if this could not be done by a meeting of the permanent members of the Security Council, then the proposal that they should meet outside the UN should not be rejected; but it would be better if they could meet as permanent members of the Security Council. I understand that General de Gaulle's proposal was that they should meet simply as four great powers. If that procedure were adopted and would bring the U.S.S.R. into the discussions, it might be useful. But I understand there are some difficulties in bringing about that meeting.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot imagine that there is anything the committee would like less at this time than a speech 
from me. I feel I have already taken up a great deal of the time of parliament talking about transport in the year 1967, and I would rather hear hon. members of the committee and listen to their suggestions before making any observations that it may be necessary for me to make.

Mr. Chairman, I am in a bit of a dilemma at this time. Two years ago the minister did not make an opening statement on his departmental estimates and things turned out unsuccessfully. Last year I suggested that if he did make a statement it might be helpful, but I do not think things turned out much more successfully last year either. So that with or without a speech we still seem to get the same result.
I should like to make one or two brief comments. I think we should recognize that considerable attention has been given to transportation generally within the period of about one full year. We looked over the departmental estimates extensively in committee slightly less than a year ago. Then we dealt with the massive transportation bill at the end of the last calendar year and the beginning of this one, when hon. members will recall that nearly every facet of transportation in this country was covered. We also had the officials of Air Canada in the committee a few weeks ago, and the Canadian National officials are to appear within a very short time. Therefore it is probably appropriate that this department is being brought forward first of all and is not one of those whose estimates are going to be sent to committee for detailed examination.
Having said this, Mr. Chairman, and having referred to the transportation bill that was brought in this year, I feel I must at the outset remind the minister that there is still one major aspect of transportation that has not been dealt with. The new bill was brought before the house and we had a successful debate. The minister had certain ideas about getting it through before Christmas but he wisely did not try to force it. It is often said that you cannot teach an old dog new tricks, but I for one think that the turning point in the legislation was before Christmas when the minister agreed to accept extensive amendments, even if this meant our consideration of the bill running into the new year. Incidentally, this advice might have been taken by the Minister of National Defence a short while ago, but that is another matter.

The minister received considerable credit at the time for this new legislation, and while there has been some delay in making appointments to the board and in taking action with regard to the preliminary work-to which I will refer later-the bill was generally received in the country as a major step forward for transportation in Canada.
However, there is one problem that was not touched on by this legislation and it has to do with an unfulfilled promise made by the minister in connection with the maritime provinces. As everyone knows, the consultants' study of our maritime transportation problems has been completed, the report is now in its final stages and will be presented before long. Even though there may be some credit due to the minister and the government for finally developing a new transportation policy as they did this year, the maritime M.P.'s-I consider I speak for all of them in that we are united on this-will not forget the study has been made and that legislation will result therefrom.
We contend that before finally any credit can be taken the minister has the solemn duty to fulfil his promise and bring about the changes that are necessary for a healthy transportation industry in the maritimes. While the minister is gadding about the country picking up honourary degrees here and there-whether they are given to him as a politician or a historian, I do not know-I would remind him that the maritime members of parliament will not rest until the report of this study is finally brought in and action on it taken by the government.
This leads me briefly to one or two matters in connection with the maritime ports, and I refer of course to the ports of Saint John and Halifax. The business in these two traditional winter ports is slipping away. I for one am not making any charges against the minister in connection with ice breaking or failing to deal with other problems that we have. There has been a tendency on the part of the government to shrug off its responsibility to see that the St. Lawrence ports receive a fair share of the business coming in and out of the country, but it is at the same time ignoring a promise that was solemnly made at confederation.

Whether he likes to admit it or not, the Diefenbaker years were good to the maritimes, and the maritimers know and appreciate that. If the government hopes to be well received in the maritimes and if he hopes to be recognized in his adopted province, action must be taken to ensure we are not left by the wayside in transport matters. The government has a responsibility for seeing that the longshoremen and others connected with the economies of Halifax and Saint John receive better treatment than has been meted out to them in the last two or three years.
I will not mention figures, but in Saint John we become very annoyed when the National Harbours Board periodically announces that a certain number of ships arrived at the port in such and such a period, giving the impression that the picture is rosy and that we may look forward to a bright future. The fact is that longshoremen's hours of work have been reduced by up to 10 per cent in the last two years. In 1966 they worked 129,446 hours less than previously- that is a lot of employment-and this year, though I have not the official figures, I understand that their employment will have decreased by 98,000 hours.
I will talk now of the grain elevator in Quebec, that the government owned. When private industry threatened to build a new elevator to compete with it, what did the government do? In effect it sold its elevator because it was afraid of competition. This is a change in government policy. The previous minister said at least twice that the National Harbours Board could run grain elevators competently; he hoped they would stay in the business, and even increase that business.
One might ask, what is the matter with selling one grain elevator at Quebec? The minister implied the answer, though it was not readily understandable, that such action relieves the government of its responsibility to see that all ports of Canada share in the grain export business. Now we have a private business operating in Quebec. I am not against private enterprise; the effect, nevertheless, of what has happened will be that private enterprise will handle more grain, and the minister will say: "I have no control over them; they are in private enterprise." Saint John and Halifax could conceivably lose much of their grain trade, which has become increasingly important because of the changes in other types of traffic I shall mention.
All the talk now is of containerization at ports, and this has become big business. Our

Supply-Transport
ports will have to be modernized and this will cost much money. The department has conducted research; nevertheless I hope the minister will explain in detail what the official thinking is about this matter. The government has a definite responsibility to enter the container business and to make the related investments. Many studies are going on, and we do not want unnecessary ones; yet I feel that the department ought to study this business of containerization in all its aspects. The government ought to decide what it will do in those ports under the jurisdiction of the National Harbours Board.
If the government does not act, big business will take its trade to ports such as New York, which have all the facilities for handling large containers. Montreal, another wealthy port, may rank second only to New York, and the maritimes will be left in the cold because facilities to handle bulk containers have not been developed there. Though Halifax competes with Saint John for business, I readily admit that Halifax has the capacity to handle large deep sea cargoes, and that Saint John has not that capacity at the moment. Container handling facilities at Halifax might be developed; nevertheless Saint John, with plenty of room behind the sheds, a favourable geographic position and four days less sailing time to Montreal, has many advantages. I say to the minister that he cannot continue to shrug off his responsibilities and hope that private enterprise or some magic wand will fulfil them. Halifax and Saint John are handling less and less modern general cargo shipments.

While on the subject, I hope there will be action on the Digby-Saint John ferry. A survey was conducted, representations were heard from communities of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and the need for the ferry established. In closing the first part of my remarks on transportation in the maritimes, I express the

hope that the minister will have an opportunity to bring us up to date on the consultants' report on transportation, to which I have referred. I know there are difficulties. The minister has taken time to get the best men he can on this board. I hope we will get far-sighted, experienced transportation experts, as well as people who have a feeling for this country and for the diverse transportation difficulties that exist. Unfortunately, I hear that some of those who have been mentioned for appointment to the board are not showing the excitement they should to accept appointment. I wish to make a brief reference to the air picture. It was alluded to in a question today, and it was stated earlier that Air Canada is having trouble with some of its services. I know Air Canada is under a great strain this year because it is being called upon for extra duty in connection with Expo, and delivery of planes is not as satisfactory as one would have wished.
At the committee hearings on Air Canada Mr. Gordon McGregor came forward in his usual straightforward manner and gave us the answers to our questions. He held nothing back, but in the final minutes of the hearing it appeared to me and most other members of the committee, when we were examining the company's budget and questioning the accountants, that Air Canada at present needs a full review and overhaul of its financial structure. I think one of the accountants said they were having trouble with their cost equity basis, or their loss equity basis. Everyone knows Air Canada goes to the C.N.R. when it wants to borrow money. It is not an independent company in the strict sense of the word.

Arrangements are made to amortize its expenditures tor the new planes which it needs for its fleet. But difficulties are now imminent in two respects. One is the giant sums of money which will be needed to finance the new SST's. In fact the company is talking in terms of $300 million. We should know exactly where the company stands as a separate entity. There is no net funded debt, and no debentures or the like to establish this. I am not an accountant, but the minister knows that now when Air Canada is in big business something has to be done. Mr. McGregor and the accountants suggested that it might be worth while to have a full study made of this question. At present the accountants are conducting a study of a minor nature, but that will not be enough.
A second reason for a full study is that Air Canada, whether it likes it or not, is now in open competition with Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I am not against C.P.A. being allowed to compete, because I think availability of choice has to be given to Canadians. The Conservative party, of which I am a member, made the breakthrough in this field and brought C.P.A. into the transcontinental picture. Although I am not against this, I think that we owe it to Air Canada, as a creature of the government, of the Canadian people, to bring it up to date and establish where it fits into the picture.
The other night many of us on the transportation committee were invited to a dinner commemorating the 25th anniversary of C.P.A. At the dinner a satellite was displayed, and I thought C.P.A. was really thinking modern. It was indicated to me that it was getting into the air business on an increasingly large scale. Although the minister was not there he may have heard that C.P.A. had three mini-skirted hostesses moving among the guests, to give us an idea of future travel and of the services of stewardesses in the future, and the thought struck me at the time that, by gosh, I should ask the Minister of Transport what he is doing about getting mini-skirts for Air Canada stewardesses. I think the minister should place high priority on this, and do something about it, himself.
Hear, hear.

The only other major topic that in my opinion deserves attention is what is called the domestic satellite communications system. I am not aware of all its implications but I know it is very important. I read the brief presented to the

Does the minister plan to have this matter referred to the transport committee? It is all tied in with the Bell Telephone representations, which will be coming before the committee this year. I shall not dwell on it now. It is a complicated subject, but it is very important for a country like Canada and we cannot afford to relax on such an important matter.

m

As the minister knows, another matter which is a favourite of mine is the St. Lawrence seaway. We want to know about the debt structure, the tolls, pollution, navigation,

height of water, levels of water and the situation in Montreal harbour. This is something which affects every part of the economic life of this country. Mr. Chairman, I believe I speak on behalf of all members present in the house when I thank the hon. member who has just taken his seat for giving us the opportunity to chuckle. He did so several minutes ago at the conclusion of a 45 to 47 minute presentation when he said he was not going to hold the house up by making a lengthy speech, but would reserve his comments for a later date. I lost track of his points after the seventeenth, but let me say that the hon. member has without doubt presented the major problems involving everything, from flowers to ports, which face the maritime provinces on the Atlantic. I know the minister will answer all the hon. member's point in detail before this consideration of his salary vote is concluded, but I should like to ask him to transfer his ministerial thinking from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast.
It is not my intention in any way to make my remarks in the nature of political criticism or comment regarding the past actions of the minister, but I should like to ask him whether it is possible under this vote to remove some of the confusion that exists so far as the Pacific coast is concerned, and give us a clear indication of what is taking place or will take place in this regard. It is about time the government recognized the potentialities of the province of British Columbia in relation to transportation and port facilities. This is very important in my opinion, and I regret having to reiterate it, as I did try to bring it to the attention of the house when I spoke during the concluding day of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Surely it cannot be challenged that the port of Vancouver, and what will be ancillary ports in the lower mainland of British Columbia, if not now, will in the near future provide not only the greatest port facilities in North America, but perhaps the greatest in the world. I make that suggestion, with the knowledge that Canadian trade will expand to a great extent in the future, particularly with eastern countries.
We are very proud of our natural resources, but I regret that far too often we export them for manufacture into articles by other countries, which in turn we import. We all hope this situation will change very soon. In this regard I hope the minister can assure us that it is government policy in respect of the export of our natural resources that they move

over Canadian transportation lines and through Canadian ports.
Although I read the newspaper reports this morning I am still not clear as to the movement of coal from the Crowsnest in British Columbia and Alberta under major contracts signed with Japanese importers. It would be a regrettable situation if the millions of tons of coal produced annually in British Columbia and Alberta were exported to Japan by way of transportation systems and ports in the United States. I sincerely hope the minister can resolve this present confusion by stating that arrangements have been made between the governments, contractors and railways for the movement of this coal production over Canadian transportation systems to Canadian harbours for export. This is a very important matter and I trust my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, does not mind my mentioning it. My second point is of particular concern to me as a member from Vancouver. At the present time about one third of the south side of the port of Vancouver falls within my constituency. After redistribution about 80 per cent will fall within the constituency of Vancouver East. Be that as it may, irrespective of the party we support, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, myself and others are concerned about the port of Vancouver. We are all anxious, because of other than political reasons to know what are the plans for the development of the port of Vancouver. This is of tremendous importance to the city of Vancouver as well as to the province.
Let me repeat what I said the other day when unfortunately the minister was not here. As a result of confusion in respect of provincial and federal jurisdictions a most serious problem is arising, and unless these jurisdictional jealousies are resolved the people of Vancouver and British Columbia are going to suffer. There has been a great deal of development in the port of Vancouver by private enterprise and there will be a great deal more in the future, particularly from the Lion's Gate bridge to Port Moody. This year as a result of plans of the harbour commissioners of the federal government the capital expenditures have been quadrupled.
Our port facilities must be enlarged because of the development of new ships of greater size for carrying cargoes of different types. Although we live under capitalism, speaking as a socialist let me say that private

enterprise is prepared to invest in this development, but there is some anxiety because of the lack of knowledge regarding future plans and the confusion in relation to jurisdiction. The provincial government under a Social Credit premier, not being satisfied with already having the largest port facilities in Canada, either existing or planned, is now considering the development of harbour facilities at Robert's bay under provincial jurisdiction and financing.
Mr. Chairman, I would urge the Minister of Transport to get in touch with the provincial authorities, the harbour commissioners and free enterprise developers regarding the future of Vancouver harbour and ancillary facilities, because unless some understanding is reached between these parties I feel we have reason to worry about the future status and financial stability, of these facilities in the province of British Columbia.
In my opinion and that of the people to whom I spoke just a few weeks ago, this situation is absolutely stupid. Unless there is a co-ordinated plan of development there will be a loss to investors, a loss to the city of Vancouver, a loss to the province of British Columbia and a loss to Canada. Empire building and jurisdictional disputes may cause millions of dollars to be spent unnecessarily in certain areas. A specific plan should first be completed in one area. To my mind this is of the utmost importance, o (12:20 p.m.)
I would ask the Minister of Transport to tell us what discussions are being carried on at the moment and, if discussions are not in progress now, what is planned for the future in order that there will be co-ordination in planning as between enterprise investment, federal government expenditure and the province with regard to the necessity of wharves, railway facilities and warehouses, so that the great port of Vancouver and the lower mainland area of British Columbia will have a development that is efficient, reasonable and satisfactory, looking ahead not only to the next few years but, I would say, for almost the next quarter of a century.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that I make this appeal not as a member of this party, not as a member of the opposition but as one who has lived in Vancouver since 1910, knows its potentialities, has faith in its future but also has real fears that our Pacific coast may lose its great potential because of challenges of jurisdiction, political expediencies and personalities between governments. I am certain

that all members of the House of Commons who come from the lower mainland of British Columbia will join me in asking the minister to inform us what he is doing in this respect and what the government has in mind to resolve the present difficulties and confusion.
I have just one other point, Mr. Chairman. I raise it because it is also a major importance. The Minister of Transport was finally able to get started on the new international airport in Vancouver. We thank him for this. That work is now proceeding. We hope that in the planning of this new airport provision is being made for the runways to handle the new types of aircraft which will be landing there in the future. I repeat what I said in the debate on the speech from the throne, because the minister was not here at that time. We from Vancouver think it is impractical and unreasonable-I do not know what the eventual cost will be, but I imagine it will be around $20 million at least-that in respect of this airport no decision has yet been made on the new access. I reiterate that I know the problems, I know the difficulties, I know the jurisdictional disputes and I know the personalities. I shall point out to the minister that he should require an investigation and not rely upon the recommendations of the Board of Transport Commissioners, since at the present time 75 per cent of its management are former employees of the C.P.R. or the C.N.R.
Automatically, the Board of Transport Commissioners has become the Senate of the railways. It is not surprising that numerous accidents occur in some places because, as always, under the pretext of economy, essential things are forgotten.
Now, I will say a few words about Air Canada. I must congratulate Air Canada for the beautiful trips we owe to it. However, times of departure, namely, should be better controlled. Here, I have in hand a card which was given to me to go aboard-I will not give the date so as not to offend the employees who were there-but, at any rate, on three occasions in the same month, I had to get off the plane leaving Montreal for Quebec. On three occasions, I had been given a boarding card.
The first night three people who had been given boarding cards had to get off because there was not a single empty seat inside the airplane.
A similar situation arose ten days later when another passenger and myself had to get off. At that time, and I point it out to the minister, it was at the end of the winter, because I was still wearing a hat and I could travel incognito. I did not use my influence as a member of parliament; I just let myself be pushed around like an ordinary citizen.
Since the same thing happened a third time, I wonder if it would not be possible to control more efficiently the list of people boarding the airplane.
Had some people boarded the plane without tickets? Are people allowed to travel standing up? If seats had been vacant, then my boarding card would have been valid. But the day when the airplane is full and three people have to get off, it is not the same thing. Supposing that the plane had been only three quarters full and that the last three people

had been allowed to board it, were there unregistered passengers inside? If so, and in case of accident, what would happen to the unregistered passengers?
Therefore, I ask the minister to investigate that matter and to take steps so that the personnel doing that work will enjoy less patronage and be stronger in arithmetic.
Fortunately, Air Canada always realizes profits which may compensate for the services provided by the C.N.R. However, I think Air Canada could take a look also at the flight schedules.
When I go to Montreal, for example, I always reserve a seat on a plane leaving rather late, around 8:30 or 9 p.m. However, if I want to leave for Montreal earlier, my name is put on the waiting list.
Three weeks ago my name was put on the waiting list for the plane leaving for Quebec at 7:30. I was made to wait at a gate and then told that there were no seats left and asked to go to gate number 7, where the other plane was leaving for Quebec. But the two planes were scheduled to leave at the same time. While I walked 50 feet inside the airport, the other plane left.
Would it not be possible to delay the departure of the second plane or move ahead that of the first? Anyway, I do not know what we could do about that, for the problem belongs to Air Canada. One plane goes directly to Quebec while the other makes a stopover at Trois-Rivieres. I think the one stopping at Trois-Rivieres could leave four or five minutes earlier or later without it making anj difference.
At any rate, that would have permitted me to leave earlier. If I insist upon this point, it is not that I had to wait in Montreal, for we are graciously welcomed, very well fed, the stewardesses are charming, in brief, it could not be better in this regard.
When I was allowed to get aboard the plane for Quebec, other passengers were refused aboard. As for me, they could not prevent me from going aboard, since I had a reservation. Nevertheless, those who were waiting could have gone aboard, if I had been given the opportunity to leave when I was ready.
That is another suggestion I am making to the minister. I presume he will get many more from other members and I can even see that the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) will certainly have a few to make also.

I hope the minister will consider all those suggestions in the best interest of the Canadian people and especially of the pocket book of the Canadian government.

Mr. Chairman, I notice in looking around the chamber now, in the lunch hour, that for the most part the hon. members who are here are members from the Atlantic and Pacific coast constituencies, and from the mountains and the prairies, because we are the ones who, when the estimates of the Minister of Transport are before the house, are most interested in this subject. To those who are present in the chamber at the moment, let me say that this is perhaps one of the most vital debates in the course of the year and an opportunity to place before the Minister of Transport some of our own ideas in respect of transport and communication to the remoter areas and the periphery of Canada; because in this thinly populated nation, holding such a vast territory, it is only by the improvement of our systems of transportation and communication that we can do our best to make possible the kind of living Canadians enjoy.
I join hon. members opposite, in particular the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, in congratulating the minister for having put in a very good year as Minister of Transport, particularly in the carriage of his massive transportation commission bill during the last session and, of special interest to us in British Columbia, the acquisition of the C.P.R. lands in the harbour of Vancouver, which broke a deadlock of decades and now permits the National Harbours Board to expand and improve the port of Vancouver in a way it could not before. This has been immediately reflected in the increased priorities given to planning in the harbour of Vancouver, and in increases in the capital expenditures of that port. This is certainly worth while to see, for those of us who have long been advocating that government initiative should break the deadlock which had long rested in the hands of the legal experts, and has now enabled the port to go ahead at a renewed and increased pace.
People in British Columbia worry about the port of Vancouver. In this statement I include my hon. friend from Vancouver East, who is disturbed by the action of the province of British Columbia in bringing down a bill in the recent session of the legislature to establish a B.C. harbours board. Certainly this is a startling piece of legislation and, one would
Supply-Transport
expect, far outside the control and jurisdiction of the province. But we know why this measure was brought down. Basically it has to do with the prospect of moving vast quantities of coal from the Kootenays, loading it on to bulk carriers at Vancouver and moving it to the smelters of Japan. The passage of this bill reflects the anxiety of the British Columbia government, lest the port of Vancouver and the facilities available through the National Harbours Board will not be adequate for this task. I think it would be a great tragedy if harbour development were to begin to take place at the instigation of two levels of government in the absence of the cohesive planning which the National Harbours Board is able to give in connection with port development.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
I certainly wish to urge at this time that the minister place his full support behind the port of Vancouver development committee. It was in 1953, or thereabouts, when the people on the north shore were wondering whether that side of the harbour would be adequately developed by the National Harbours Board, and struggling with the question of settling the long dispute over the C.P.R. lands so that the port could expand, that the port of Vancouver development committee was established.
It was the present Minister of Transport who met with representatives of the city of Vancouver and listened to their proposals for the establishment of a port development committee, which has worked very well ever since. It has produced some useful reports and background help to the National Harbours Board in planning transportation on the Pacific coast. I wish to emphasize the value of this committee which was established by the present minister, and ask him to consider carefully whether he is providing that committee with sufficient expertise to enable it to carry out the job it wants to do-for example, in determining whether or not we should be building bulk loaders on the mainland or whether they could be contained inside the harbour.
I want the minister to consider whether or not the committee is receiving all the help it needs to carry out this expert, high level planning and to get its ideas before the government and before the people of the west coast who are constantly worried about what is in store in the long run for the port city. We hear on the one hand from the British Columbia government that we need extra

May 26, 1967
Supply-Transport
loading facilities outside the port of Vancouver. On the other hand, strangely enough, we find that a vessel called the Sigsilver was able to dock and load in the port without difficulty, despite its heavy tonnage.
Mr. Chairman, the Sigsilver sailed under the first narrows bridge on its first maiden voyage. Its size was such that it virtually blocked the view of Grouse mountain and the north shore. Yet this vessel, a vessel of 103,021 tons which draws a maximum of 49 feet of water, and is 820 feet 2 inches long and 133 feet 10 inches wide, tied up in the port, loaded 73,000 tons of grain and sailed out again. This was a spectacle which set the city of Vancouver on its tin ear. We witnessed it, while Mr. Bennett was telling us that what we need today is to go outside the port of Vancouver and dig a big new harbour. I am not convinced in the least that Mr. Bennett is right. I am frightened that if he goes ahead with this project-though I do not see how he can, within the powers given him under the British North America Act-we in British Columbia will face an increase in taxation the like of which we have never seen, in return for a project which would prove a white elephant the like of which we have never seen.
This is why I believe the port of Vancouver development committee should be beefed up with all the technical assistance it needs, and afforded every opportunity to express its views to the government and to the people so that they may understand where we are going and not foolishly undertake the construction of a white elephant at a time when we need to develop our port intelligently, with dollars spent to the best purpose and in the best interests of the people of the west coast, the prairies and the country generally.
I wish to mention now a subject which has been drawn to my attention by people in Vancouver who are very much concerned about the dumping of garbage by pleasure boats and small craft using the strait of Georgia, which is a small inland sea about 20 miles across from Vancouver island. It is likely that more pleasure boats sail in this area than in any other area around our shores, coastal or inland. As our wealth grows and our leisure increases, the number of small craft sailing in this area is increasing at a tremendous rate. All kinds of new facilities are needed, and the use of these craft needs to be brought under a certain measure of control because the point is being reached at which they are begining to pollute the strait of Georgia.
[Mr. Deachman.l
Garbage is washing up on beaches where people have built permanent homes and cottages. Before these practices become entrenched I want to draw the situation in the strait to the attention of the minister. I know he has taken one step for which we in British Columbia will be grateful. He has appointed a highly respected member of his staff to make a survey of the needs of small boat harbours. It may be that the terms of reference governing that survey need to be widened to cover the whole question of how best to deal with the massive increase in the numbers of small vessels which plow up and down this inland waterway.
I wish to turn for a moment now to the subject of the Vancouver airport. I hope the minister will be able to tell us how the construction of this airport is progressing. Each time we visit Vancouver we see the framework of the new airport building progressing. We are anxious to know when the building and the runways will be available for use. We are just as anxious to know what solution will be found to the knotty question of providing an access tunnel or bridge to the new airport.
I have letters in front of me from the Vancouver Real Estate Board, the Marpole Chamber of Commerce, the chamber of commerce of the lower mainland and from the B.C. Towboat Owners Association, all expressing concern about the crossing of the north arm of the Fraser river, the arm of the Fraser river which leads to the sea. It is used intensively by large traffic, and each year, as bigger barges are built, the clearance required in both width and depth continues to increase. Industry is naturally concerned therefore about the kind of bridge which would be built. This is a question which has to be settled without delay, because intending passengers will want to get to the airport quickly. We want to see the airport completed speedily, and we want this connection to be made as soon as the airport can be opened. I realize this raises once again a jurisdictional problem as between the two levels of government; but there are good reasons why these jurisdictional disputes should be settled to enable us to get on with the work.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I want to refer to one item I had a little bit to do with at the time the transportation commission bill was passed. It involves the movement of feed grains into British Columbia and the rail rates which apply to their movement. A clause was introduced into the
May 26, 1967

bill at the time which indicated that this subject would come up for review within six months of the establishment of the commission. The farmers who were feeding stock in British Columbia raised this issue with members from British Columbia and asked that it be brought up at the time the bill was before the house, and they are anxious to know when this matter is likely to be attended to in the future. They will want to make representations at that time, and therefore they would like to know how to make those representations and when to make them.
I should like to compliment the minister as well as Air Canada upon the establishment of a new DC-9 service from Ottawa through Winnipeg and Calgary to Vancouver. This is a considerable improvement over the former service where we had to go through Toronto. We always had to wait at Toronto airport for at least an hour and a half and often longer in order to make a connection to the coast. Certainly the new service speeds up communication with the coast and adds an additional line which is very useful indeed to members and government officials who are travelling to and from the prairies and the coast.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few remarks about the question of a communications satellite which I think was a matter raised earlier in the debate today. I hope the minister will say something about this. There are just three points that I want to make about a communications satellite, a subject that I find pretty fascinating.
We in Canada with not too much expense to the individual could put our dial telephones on a flat rate basis with the use of a satellite, and this would mean that any Canadian could pick up his telephone and dial the user of any other dial telephone in Canada. This could be done on a flat rate basis, as I say, at not too great a charge on a subscriber's present bill.
Satellite communication would not only assist in the increase and broadening of such a service, but it would also-and perhaps this is the most fascinating part about it-enable telephone service to be provided to virtually every corner of Canada, even to the north pole if somebody was up there with a telephone in his hand. I think this would be a magnificent addition to the capability of Canadians to communicate with each other.
Communication, Mr. Chairman, is not really costly compared with many other things we do. It is not as costly, say, as building railroads, roads, canals, or even icebreaking,
Supply-Transport
as pointed out by my hon. friend for Saint John-Albert. It is an area in which we can afford to go far beyond what is done by other countries, even the United States. It is essential to a great country like this, which covers such tremendous area, that we communicate with each other and do everything we possibly can in this connection.
I might also point out that a satellite is capable of providing us with television on a virtually universal basis. I do not see why Canadians have to be slaves either to United States programs or to C.B.C. and local programs. I do not see why we cannot become the first country in the world to make available to its people virtually universal television coverage by bringing to Canadian viewers via a satellite network programs from Moscow, Paris, London, and even Peking, if they want to talk to us or harangue us.
I see nothing wrong with letting the Canadian people see what goes on in world through universal T.V., and this can be provided with a satellite. We have the facilities to do it and, again, it is not something that will be too expensive. It is a great dream, the kind of vision that Canadians, of all people, can afford to dream about.
This concludes, Mr. Chairman, the points I want to make in this address today. It has certainly been a pleasure to me to have been a member of the transportation committee over the last two years and to have had the opportunity to confront the minister and members of crown corporations and find out something about their various operations.
Mr. Chairman, on looking at the clock I would ask the permission of the committee to adjourn this debate until after lunch.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity of speaking on the transport estimates. Before going further I wish to compliment the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, the official spokesman for our group on the transport and communications committee, for his comprehensive briefing of the

May 26, 1967
Supp ly-Transport
minister before lunch on the problems now facing Canadian transportation. The hon. member complimented the minister for successfully piloting through the house the massive transportation bill. As a member of the committee I second what the hon. member said. The legislation was most important and we appreciated the minister's co-operation. It took a big, forward step in bringing our transportation legislation up to date. Nevertheless the benefits of the legislation will not be realized unless in the near future the new transport board is set up. That is the most important initial step which ought to be taken. To solve our transportation difficulties the new board ought to be set up at once and fully manned.
We realize that the minister is having a difficult time, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert suggested, in obtaining appropriate personnel for the board. Nevertheless the board must be set up and fully constituted if it is to decide on transportation matters. Setting up the board is the first step which ought to be taken, and it ought to be taken immediately.
I have in my hand a copy of a letter written by Mr. G. P. Miller, solicitor for the Canadian Pacific, to approximately 125 reeves, councillors, town clerks, etc. of various places in the Regina subdivision in that part of Saskatchewan. The letter refers to a large segment of the communications system of that part of our province and to an application for the removal of station agents -carrying through, in other words, the Canadian Pacific proposal for the establishment of a master agency plan.
I need not tell members of the committee or the minister that consternation will develop in the near future among the people of this part of Saskatchewan should the application for the removal of so many agents from so wide an area be granted. I shall mention a few of the many municipalities involved and try not to bore the committee. At the head of the list is Grenfell, followed by places such as Indian Head, Stoughton, Carlyle, Rouleau, Torquay, Wolseley, Qu'Appelle, Fillmore, Redvers, Areola, Milestone, Imperial and Midale. These are all important centres of railroad communication in this part of Saskatchewan, and removing the station agents in one fell swoop from such a large area would create many difficulties. This application ought not to be considered for a minute until the new board has been fully constituted, and I urge the minister to allow these

municipalities a hearing before the board, after it is set up, before the requests in the application are granted.
That is only one part of the difficulty. As members of the committee know, the railways accepted the suggestion of the MacPherson Royal Commission that they apply to the Board of Transport Commissioners to abandon certain rail lines. These applications to abandon were reviewed in depth. Here, again, I think the minister did right, prior to the full implementation of the transportation bill, in applying a moratorium on applications seeking to abandon some 2,200 miles of line. This action has in a way poured oil on the troubled waters for the time being and established in the minds of the people of western Canada that there is not going to be wholesale abandonment of lines. But it still left about 1,800 miles of line to be considered, and immediately the bill was passed there was a rush by the railroads with applications to abandon these 1,800 miles of lines. Approximately 900 miles of these lines lie within the boundaries of Saskatchewan, and once more I urge the minister to have the greatest concern regarding the final outcome of these abandonment applications.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I believe we should have retention committees established again and complete hearings before any of these applications are granted. As hon. members know, as one vitally interested in the problem of rail line abandonment I have had a private members' bill on the order paper for the last several years to provide that if a particular segment of line is to be abandoned following application the abandonment shall not take place until the expiration of at least a five-year moratorium. I introduced that bill for the simple reason that railroads are a vital part of the community life of the rural areas of Saskatchewan. This is true of other provinces as well but it is particularly applicable to the west where the transportation of our grain is one of the basic responsibilities of railroads.
In many of the small towns and villages through which railway lines run the general store caters to the needs of the surrounding area. In many cases it houses the post office. These small villages may contain a garage repair shop which repairs the machinery of the local farmers, and the owners of these places should have a reasonable time within which to pull up stakes, dispose of their property and make arrangements to establish themselves in some other form of livelihood.
May 26, 1967

There is also the question of the elevator companies which provide services to farmers along the railway lines. Their owners should have time to dismantle the elevators, move them elsewhere and make arrangements for their former patrons.
When railway lines are abandoned the municipalities affected are faced with the responsibility of providing transportation facilities involving the construction of better roads. If there were a five year moratorium on abandonments this would allow provincial and municipal governments three or four years in which to plan ahead in order to find the tax money for the building of roads. Again I suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to these matters before further action is taken on rail line abandonment.
Under the new transport legislation we tried to establish the concept that rates would be set by competition in the market place. I believe in this principle of free enterprise, but with reasonable controls and with people being realistic about the establishment of rates. It has recently come to my attention that already, before the new board has been able to start functioning, rates have been hiked in several areas of western Canada in what are known as captive zones. Rates have been raised by both the C.N. and C.P.R., and the increases in both cases have been uniform.
We do not know whether this is due to collusion between the railroads or whether it has happened by accident, but when one finds exactly the same increase being made by two railroads, both in areas where they have no competition and where they have competition, one begins to wonder what is taking place. This indicates to me that the sooner the new transportation commission starts functioning, and the sooner it receives competent, expert advice, the better it will be for all of us. Precedents should not be established now that will be hard to overcome if a problem develops along the lines I am suggesting.
During the past several months questions have been raised in Saskatchewan about air transportation services in the province. Because of Expo and because of the fact that this is Canada's one hundredth birthday, there is a great demand for air services and all other modes of transport. Because Saskatchewan is so far away from the site of Expo, in order to save time many people want to use air transport to reach it. People are now finding difficulty making reservations for plane transportation to and from eastern Canada, and I wonder whether the minister,
Supply-Transport
in co-operation with Air Canada, Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and the private companies, have given enough consideration to this problem in Saskatchewan.
Just before the last session prorogued I had a question on the order paper dealing with the landing of jet aircraft at Regina, and I believe the minister's parliamentary secretary suggested that the facilities at Regina were capable of handling jet transport. But up to the present time I am not aware of any jet aircraft coming into Regina, unless I have not been briefed on the situation within the last week or two. It may be possible that jet aircraft can land there, and I suggest that Regina and Saskatoon should be serviced by DC-9 jet planes to give the people of central Canada comparable facilities with those provided to people elsewhere.
I could go on at some length to deal with other matters pertaining to transportation. However, this morning the hon. member for Saint John-Albert covered 17 or 18 pertinent points relating to the various facets of transportation problems. We all realize that transportation is the sinew of this great nation, and the more we can do to improve transportation facilities the better service we do our country. With these few remarks I would again urge the minister to do everything within his power to see that the new transport board is constituted and becomes active as soon as possible so that it can deal with some of the problems that are creeping up on us and which, if not dealt with, could create dangers and give rise to precedents that would cause a lot of concern later.

Mr. Chairman, I want to begin my remarks by trying to say a few words in English. All hon. members know that most of the time I speak French, my mother tongue, because I am somewhat more fluent in it, but I purposely begin in English today because I want to demonstrate that in my constituency, in my province, there is none of that narrow-minded jingoism that we have observed here during the last few weeks, demonstrated by the hon. member for York-Humber. If we have a few exceptions to the general rule, our people at least do not send them to the House of Commons; they keep them at home. We have an example of course, in the person of the hon. member for Lapointe, but he is serving here under false colours. He was elected by Le Ralliement Creditiste and his colleagues had the intelligence to throw him out of the party when he changed his colours.
Supply-Transport

May 26, 1987
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
(Translation)
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I shall continue in my mother tongue, in which I will certainly be a little more fluent.
I must admit that the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has a lot of very important problems to solve-problems of the ten provinces-so that is why we are obliged, in many cases, to bring up again those which seem important in our ridings. I shall make a brief digression to say that:

I will repeat it in English. I resented the remarks of the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Quadra this morning when he said that members from the maritimes and British Columbia were more interested in the problems of the Minister of Transport than other members. I should like to tell my hon. friend that those of us who live along the St. Lawrence river are also keenly interested. We are even very interested in what is going on in the maritimes and in British Columbia, because we believe in solidarity between the provinces.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to apologize to the hon. member. I was using the word "maritime" in the broad sense. His constituency like mine is a maritime constituency.

I thank my hon. colleague. I believe he realizes mine is a friendly resentment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. Minister of Transport for his attentive co-operation every time I rose in this house to ask for an emergency night service of the Canadian Pacific between Montreal and Quebec during Expo. I had the impression that the minister was one of the strong men in the cabinet but, to my great regret, he just found people stronger that he, in the person of the president and vice-president of the Canadian Pacific who seem to have an extraordinary power of resistance, since they resisted even to the pressure of the Minister of Transport.
Mr. Chairman, I should tell the minister that not later than today at noon I had another telephone conversation with the staff of the Canadian Transport Commission who advised me that they were maintaining the pressure and were hoping to bring around the authorities of the C.P.R. Consequently, for a few

days we will need the support of the Minister of Transport. I hope we can count on his support and this afternoon, I urge him to give us as strong a support as possbile so that, this time, we may win our point.
To some extent the interest of the Montreal Expo is at stake since there are between Montreal and Quebec approximately one million interested people who cannot easily visit Expo because our roads, our bus service and our air transport facilities are totally inadequate.
Only the railroad can bring in our people in the morning and bring them back at night. I have a full file that I shall not read to the house because the C.P.R. could try to fight my request-which is supported by the legislature of my province and by a large number of municipalities

by producing statistics on the number of train passengers during the month of March.
For instance, train No. 152 carried 1,960 passengers from March 1 to 21 compared with 1,261 between March 22 and March 31. This is between Montreal and Quebec. Previously, train No. 149 had carried 1,638 passengers from March 1 to March 21 and 1,057 passengers from March 22 to March 31.
Those are figures gathered before the opening of Expo, and I contend that if we had the service we are requesting, those figures would increase considerably during the next six months. By the way, I know that the municipal councils of my region are ready to publicize this and the newspapers of my region are also ready to give free publicity to that penurious company called the C.P.R.
I also know that all the radio commentators in my area would be most happy to broadcast the idea that the C.P.R. has finally realized they should render some service to the people after the enormous amounts they have collected from the population at the time the company was founded.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I refuse to have the C.P.R. tell us that no cars are available, because I actually know that there are some unused cars in Montreal that could leave at night and return the next morning without disturbing anyone.
I deny the allegation of the C.P.R. that the service would be uneconomic, and I would like to be able to prove it. If there are no passengers-and I admit they are maybe too few-it is because of the poor service provided by the C.P.R.
May 26. 1967

If the C.P.R. treated its passengers as well
as ordinary private enterprises that are subject to competition, the number of passengers would increase and the service would be economic.
I insist on this point, and ask the minister to give priority to this urgent problem, because Expo is already opened and hundreds of people tell me that they would like to leave for Montreal in the morning with their families and come back at night after having seen all the wonderful exhibits. The train is the only available means of transportation, because automobiles are impractical; besides, most people do not own an automobile.
I now come to a matter which may be of greater interest to the Minister of Transport, because I want to deal with the harbour of Trois-Rivieres which the Maritimers consider as a competitor.
However, we are witnessing a strange phenomenon, Mr. Chairman. In recent years, we have been happy to see the St. Lawrence river open to winter navigation right up to Trois-Rivieres. This was excellent for our economy. But this year we are sorry to see that the minister went beyond the call of duty in his efforts to open up the St. Lawrence, for winter navigation is now possible right up to Montreal and no longer stops at Trois-Rivieres. The people in the maritimes now see the price that must be paid for progress; they have suffered from it just as we are suffering now. However, we believe that things will straighten out and that we will also in the end benefit reasonably from this winter traffic on the St. Lawrence river without, of course, taking away the livelihood of the maritime provinces.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I think that, on the contrary, it is appropriate to consider the advantages which that whole field offers and to try all together to promote shipping as well as foreign trade, so that the volume of traffic will increase to the benefit of all.
I would like to ask the minister if he could elaborate a master plan, that is to say a plan under which the development of the Trois-Rivieres harbour and town planning would go hand in hand.
Mr. Chairman, we have a wonderful view on one of the most beautiful rivers in the world, the St. Lawrence river, but unfortunately the warehouses on the wharves are slowly becoming a China wall between the river and the city. It is certainly the most beautiful area of the city of Trois-Rivieres and I am wondering if there is not some way
Supply-Transport
to reconcile the two, for instance to elaborate a plan which would provide for the construction over the buildings, in co-operation with the municipality or the province, of walks so that the people of the Trois-Rivieres area will be able to keep that beautiful view on the St. Lawrence.
I cannot see why this beautiful scenery should be destroyed by the inexorable development of trade in the country. There is certainly a way to elaborate a town planning program and the Board of Transport Com-missionners could work with the responsible people in order to find a way to reconcile the two and to preserve all the picturesque value of that view.
I feel the whole population of the St. Maurice region and all the tourists would benefit from it. Some thought might also be given to the development of the harbour which has been slightly hampered by the construction of the bridge at Trois-Rivieres. We shall not bring up again the differences of opinion with regard to its location.
I feel that would compel the government to plan, although it may already do so without being aware of it, the development around Trois-Rivieres West and Cap-de-la-Madeleine in the next 25 years, because the regional economy due to the building of that bridge and several other developments back home, will certainly boom in the years ahead. Harbour facilities should not follow the boom; they should precede it to a certain extent, in order to increase it if possible.
I also remind the minister that during the war of 1914-18, Trois-Rivieres had a dry dock. It was closed after the end of the war. To my mind, it might be a good idea to open it again; it could be done at little cost.
Some dredging might be necessary in the northeastern St. Maurice, near Cap-de-la-Madeleine where it used to be. I think that minor repairs to pleasure boats could keep quite a number of workers busy in that area during the winter.
Besides, I think that all we have in shipyards at present cannot meet the ever-increasing demand for ship repairs, and I submit to the minister that a study should be made by experts in his department with a view to promoting the industrial and economic development of the region I represent.
Perhaps it is not necessary to wait for that to start dredging that branch of the river -there is only one river back home, not three, but because there are two cities, there are three mouths-where the drydock was

May 26, 1967
Supply-Transport
formerly and which is now used as a refuge by yachts and vessels working on the St. Lawrence. Unfortunately, that is filled in each year and those people need dredging to get into that mouth of the river.
Mr. Chairman, I almost got carried away when I talked about the C.P.R. There is one other question which makes my blood pressure go up every time I think of it, because people in my riding write to me ten times a month about it. I refer to the matter of Baie-Jolie, which the minister heard about. A channel was dredged in lake St. Peter, which was necessary of course and all the earth that was taken out of the channel was dumped in front of a beautiful beach called Baie-Jolie. More than 40 or 50 years ago, the people of Trois-Rivieres built summer cottages there, magnificent summer homes. Not only temporary cottages.
Some of those residences cost more than $60,000 and $70,000. A kind of Sahara desert was built in front of their beach and if even one could see golden sand there, it would be bearable, but it is more or less dried up mud.
The hon. minister was kind enough to answer several of my letters. I sent many to him and he answered me, for instance, as follows on October 17:
-I can well understand the disappointment of the land owners in seeing that the final result does not come up to their expectation-
I am quoting word for word.
-but it seems there are no steps the Department of Transport can take in the circumstances and at the present time in order to cope with the situation.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is the Department of Transport that is to blame. I am sorry to say so but that is the case. And the Department of Transport is trespassing; it took it for granted that the beach was its property. But under the old French law, riparian owners own not only the beach but as far under the river as the breast of a white horse. That is written in the old French law.
Therefore, these riparian owners have been greatly wronged. I have here a list, Mr. Chairman, of the owners with their signature. I have the appraisal of their property which they have had prepared, and a professional appraiser certified that their property has been depreciated as much as 40 per cent.
I think that the minister has been misinformed by some senior officials who have thus made a serious blunder, and have done a great deal of damage to these wonderful properties. I see no other solution for the

department than to make good that mistake, and so much the worse for those who committed it.
Suggestions have been made such as, for instance, to dig a channel between the old beach and this sort of mud desert created in front of their properties. But I say that this is not reasonable. To begin with, the channel will fill every year; the department will have to maintain it in good condition.
Suggestion was also made to fill up that sort of channel which is there at high tide; but here again, that will create more or less a swamp.
To my mind, there is only one solution, and that is to spread this earth on all the neighbouring beaches, try to bring in some sand so that it will not look like mud and repair the damage to these owners who did not ask for this. They were not consulted before this refuse was dumped opposite the properties which they have kept beautiful for the past 20, 25, 30 and 40 years and in which they themselves invested a lot of money.
I find the situation most regrettable. If the hon. minister could, one morning, for example, manage to fly over this area with me-it would take half an hour to get there by government plane, half an hour to examine the site and another half hour to come back -I am convinced he would come back to Ottawa shocked at what he had seen, how intelligent engineers can spoil a site so badly.
I insist on this point, Mr. Chairman, because in my region this has become a notorious scandal which manifests itself in many ways; I shall give the minister one last example.
I have just sent a questionnaire to the people in my region, asking them whether they would rather see me affiliate with the Liberal party than remain an independent. I will show the minister the results.
However, in spite of the results of the past few years, I maintain that my home town is Liberal minded. But it is a Liberal town where the Liberals are disappointed about many things. Even if it were just to correct some blunders made in the past, I think that we should give some consideration to the needs of those people, try to make them feel that at least the Liberals, 1967 model are an improvement over some former types who did not seem to care much about the needs of our people.
I, for one, would put the hon. minister in that improved category of members of the Liberal party.
May 26, 1967

Obviously, that is not the essential point of my argument. However, it still represents the frame of mind of our people at the present time because, once more, several mistakes have been made and that is one of them.
Mr. Chairman, I now conclude my remarks so as not to take advantage of the patience of the minister even if he is a model of patience. In fact, he proved it to us on several occasions, in particular during consideration of his bill on the Board of Transport Commission-ners. I would not want to go as far as awarding him a martyr's crown, but I ask him once again to take ultimate, vigorous and unprecedented steps to help us solve the problem of the night train between Montreal and Quebec City, as well as the deplorable situation known as the problem of Baie-Jolie.
As to the development plans for the harbour of Trois-Rivieres, which, incidentally, is the most paying harbour in Canada-whether my friends of all the other provinces like it or not, proportionately speaking, of course, it is the most paying harbour for the National Harbours Board-I need not say any more. The minister will realize that the entire economy of the very core of Quebec is at stake. I hope that, before long, comprehensive development plans will be drawn up for the next 25 years, while taking into account town planning which should not be overlooked in our area.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by congratulating the minister on his honorary degrees. I am most impressed that he should receive three doctorates in such a short time. I do not want to allow any envy to show through my delight, but as another member who left the ivy halls for the rocky road of politics and thereby gave up the opportunity to earn degrees I must admit I did have a touch of envy. I have often thought that perhaps for one like myself a grand slam would be an appointment to the Senate and a little slam would be an honorary degree. The minister is likely to attain both of these and I, alas, may not attain either. Perhaps he will remember me as he becomes an alumnus of more and more universities.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
As others have said before, and this is indeed a truism, transportation is always an important part of the discussions in this house. Indeed transportation has always been important in Canada. I do not know whether
Supply-Transport
one could go as far as Sir Francis Hincks did and say that railways are politics. But there would have been no Canada and no confederation if at the very beginning governments had not become involved in the transportation business in a very big way. This applies to left wing parties, right wing parties and middle of the road parties, if there are any such around. It is not just to British Columbia that transportation has meant a great deal. Undertakings were given, as a part of the confederating process, to other members of what is now the dominion. Some of those undertakings have not been honoured, and in other cases services were provided at an inadequate and unsatisfactory level.
One thing that has always troubled me as a maritimer is why Canadian National Railways is not, in terms of passenger service, truly transcontinental, why a passenger cannot get on a train at Halifax, get a berth or bedroom or whatever he can or cannot afford and go across the country.
Mr. Chairman, did the hon. gentleman say "Halifax"?
Yes, I said "Halifax".
Halifax is well into the middle of the country, as I am sure the hon. gentleman realizes.

I said that I was speaking as a maritimer, and the minister should know that the people of his adopted province do not like the expression "maritimes"; they prefer "Atlantic Canada". But the point is well taken, except that the gauge of the railway might destroy my case. I still contend that a Haligonian should be able to take a bedroom and get to Vancouver on the train. I wish to deal specifically with the removal of agencies on the Canadian National system and in particular the removal of the agency at Coniston, all brought about because the Canadian National in implementing its master agency development plan is centralizing its agency system.
Though Coniston is a small town of approximately 3,000 people it is closely linked to a portion of suburban Sudbury and serves a large farming community to the northeast. Some who live 25 to 30 miles from Sudbury protested the closing of the Coniston agency as they conducted much business through it.

Pye, commission counsel, wrote this letter which was referred to my office by Mr. C. W. Rump, Secretary of the Board of Transport Commissioners. As part of the master agency development on the northern Ontario area, on October 18, 1965, all services formerly provided from our Coniston

agency were transferred to our Sudbury office. The agent at Coniston has been retained with train order duties only, and will be retained until an application is made to the board for formal closing of the station along with a number of other points on the northern Ontario area.

This is what happens to C.N.R. business when they experiment with this type of centralizing of agencies.

The hearing was to commence at two o'clock on February 22, but at ten o'clock in the morning there was a knock at the door of the residential part of the station, and when the agent went to the door he was asked if he had moved all his belongings out of the station. When he inquired why, he was told that men had arrived that morning with instructions to start demolishing the station-on the very day the hearing was to be held to decide whether or not the agency at Coniston was to be closed.

It is typical of the C.N.R. that when they start on a project of this nature they go at it from all angles. They eliminate services. They started out in this case by phasing out the handling of express and freight at Coniston station. They let the station get into such a deplorable state that nobody wanted to patronize the place at all. However, in spite of the fact that they made every attempt to phase out the business at Coniston there is one very interesting fact I would like to put on record, namely, that in September, 1965, when actually all business was phased out at Coniston station, the revenue of that station for that month was $26,072.63. In the same month of the previous year the revenue was only $15,117.85. Further, in spite of the fact that the railway discontinued all business at the agency in September, 1965, total revenue for that year at the station was $238,197.15 compared with $198,716.45 for the previous year.
When revenues were decidedly on the increase, in spite of the fact that the C.N.R. let the station get into a deplorable condition and actually discouraged patronage by cutting off passenger service, express service and the like, it is pretty hard to explain to the people of Coniston why the C.N.R. saw fit to remove the station. I think this is typical of what is going on all across the Canadian National system. I have had many letters and complaints from people involved in this sort of thing. It seems to me the backroom boys in the C.N.R. are more interested in setting up a tight little system within their own organization which works to their advantage than they are in anything else. They do not give a hoot about service to the public. Yet what are the railways for but to provide transportation services and facilities to the public?
One cannot overlook the employees in this situation. The agent at Coniston is an example. He is practically out of a job. He has a daughter who needs constant medical care. The only other job he can take is 600 miles away from availability of that type of care, and so he is left high and dry.
In addition to cancelling the agency at Coniston the C.N.R. also made application for cancellation of the agency at Burwash on the same subdivision. When one looks at the recommendations of the board following its visit to Coniston, one wonders just what on earth it was driving at.
The board has gone along with the application of the C.N.R., but has included a recommendation to grant what it calls some measure of relief. It has recommended that a resident caretaker be appointed who will be in attendance at the station, to "execute all duties with respect to the handling of express traffic." How is there going to be any express traffic when the station goes? Further, it has recommended that the caretaker "keep the station clean, heated and lighted when necessary for the accommodation of traffic." What traffic? This is a real joke. How can there be any traffic when no trains stop there? The place is also in such a filthy state that I do not know how anyone could clean it up.
Supply-Transport
The board also recommends that the caretaker "take care of L.C.L. freight shipments." How can there be any such shipments when they are being sent under the authority of the C.N.R. to Sudbury? I hope the minister will look into this matter. I am sure that if the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. made a little effort to clean up their stations and provide the necessary services their revenues would increase. If this were done at Coniston there would be need for an agent there for a long time to come.
