Mr. Chairman, a year ago, in February 1966, I spoke on the supply resolutions of the Department of Transport. At that time I devoted some considerable time going into detail regarding the water level of lake Ontario, because this has been a problem to the people living in the lake Ontario basin for some years past. A year ago, in commenting on the situation, I congratulated the Secretary of State for External Affairs for what had been accomplished by February 1966, namely, that the water level of lake Ontario had risen 2.7 feet in one year following unlimited protests by the people on both sides of lake Ontario, in the United States and Canada, about the fact that the water levels were not being maintained under the authority of the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act and under the direction of the International Joint Commission. The protests on this point were based on the fact that there were in February 1966, have been for some years and are now, two dams across the St. Lawrence river, one at Iroquois and one at Cornwall. Both of these dams can control the water level of lake Ontario if they are closed and if attention is paid to the water level of lake Ontario.
The burden of our protest last year was that the dam at Iroquois never is closed and the power interests are allowed to draw off all the water they want at Cornwall despite the effect it may have on the water level of lake Ontario. Today, when we are considering the estimates of the Department of Transport we have every reason to congratulate the Minister of Transport for the fine level of lake Ontario today. We wish also to commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs because we know he has taken an active part in seeing that the International Joint Commission paid more attention to the International Boundary Waters Act than they had paid to it for several years previously.

May 26, 1967
Supply-Transport
During the 94 years from 1861, when the records were first kept, until 1955 when the first work was done on the St. Lawrence Seaway, the average level of lake Ontario was 244.78 feet. This was the average level of lake Ontario when the water was flowing freely down the St. Lawrence river impeded only by the Long Sault rapids and the islands between Kingston and Montreal.
When protesting about the level of lake Ontario last year and the year before that, when there were two dams across the St. Lawrence river, I pointed out in no uncertain terms that in 1965 the water level of lake Ontario was so low in Toronto harbour, according to the report of the harbour commission, that it was within one quarter inch of the all time low ever recorded in Toronto harbour since records have been maintained. As of today, May 26, 1967, the water level in Toronto harbour is 245.8 feet. I should like to state that all the people who are interested in shipping in Lake Ontario and the Toronto harbour area are very pleased with this water level of 245.8 feet. It compares favourably with the 94 year average-the period which ended in 1955-of 244.78 feet. So, today we have one more foot of water than the average level for the 94 year period.
In rising to comment on this situation, I do so because May is the second highest month in the year in respect of water levels in lake Ontario, June being the top month for high water levels. I should like to ask that the Minister of Transport be certain to see these dams are kept in a control position at Iroquois and Cornwall so that the water level of lake Ontario will not be allowed to sink below the 94 year average of 244.78 feet. We are one foot above that average today. I was told by the officials at the Department of Transport this morning on my way to the buildings that the mean level of lake Ontario for 1966 was 244.55 feet, according to the international great lakes data. The 1966 level of 244.55 feet is below the 94 year average of
244.78	feet.
Now, in the month of May, we have a water level in lake Ontario of 245.8 feet and have two dams on the St. Lawrence river which should play an important part in maintaining the water level at a figure equal to or above the 94 year average. The people in the basin will not be satisfied to see the level of lake Ontario drop below the average level for the 94 year period. Even if the power interests scream that they must have the water through the dams, they must be told by the

International Joint Commission, on which the United States and Canadian governments are represented, that they will have to restrict the use of power rather than drop the water level of lake Ontario below the 94 year average of
244.78	feet.
One of the most interesting sections in the International Boundary Waters Treaty is article 8. I have read this in the house before and I want to read it again because I appeared before the external affairs committee on the days when Mr. A. D. P. Heeney, the then chairman of the International Joint Commission appeared. I asked him a number of questions at that time concerning the enforcement of the International Boundary Waters Act. Hon. members might be interested to look at this evidence. I mentioned to him that the first use for water as set out in the international agreement between Canada and the United States is for domestic and sanitary purposes and, second, if there is sufficient water, for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation. Then, the third use is for power and irrigation purposes.
It is interesting, in respect of this third point, the use of water for power, to note that we have the hydro people of Ontario and a prominent member of the Ontario legislature running around the country saying that the use of water for power has a high position in the international boundary waters agreement between the United States and Canada. They say it has a high position, being in third position. They do not point out that there are only three positions in the agreement and that the use of water for power is the third and last. They emphasize that it has a high position. Mr. Heeney, in my presence, said that the use of water must be divided equitably. Mr. Heeney was only chairman of the International Joint Commission. I understand that since then he has retired by reason of reaching age 65.
I should like to point out that there is nothing in the agreement between Canada and the United States which mentions equitable division of use of water. There is a table which sets out the priority for the use of water and the first use is for domestic and sanitary purposes. The second use is for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation, and the third is for power and for irrigation purposes.

I should like to emphasize to the Minister of Transport that now, after waiting two
May 26, 1967

years, the people in the Lake Ontario basin have finally achieved a water level of 245.8 feet as of today. He should see that it is maintained above this 94 year average of
244.78	feet in order to live up to the terms of the international boundaries water agreement and to observe the table of usage as set out by the international agreement. If there are people downstream yelling that they must have more water, they are in an unfortunate position because they are downstream. The people on Lake Ontario have the first use of the water and the dams at Cornwall and Iroquois should be used to control the level of Lake Ontario.
In referring to the levels of Lake Ontario I do so with the definite intention of suggesting to the Minister of Transport that the Liberal party must give serious consideration to the question of erecting dams at Sarnia, Am-herstburg and Fort Erie to control the water levels in Lake Huron, Lake Michigan, Lake St. Clair, the Detroit River and Lake Erie.
Expo has given a tremendous shot in the arm to business throughout Canada, and particularly in eastern Canada. When Expo closes in October, without question there will be a tremendous letdown to industrial and business activity in that area. Many industries and business are benefiting at the present time from the great activity engendered by Expo and centennial celebrations.
This nation should be engaged in another great enterprise such as the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the financing of the original component part of the Canadian National Railway, the building of the St. Lawrence Seaway, or the erecting of many national monuments such as those I mentioned. One of the great international activities that the United States and Canada should engage in quicky is a program for the control of water levels of Lake Huron and Lake Michigan, by the building of a great international dam at Sarnia.
We could also establish water levels for Lake St. Clair, the Detroit River and control the level of Lake Erie, always bearing in mind that the use of water as agreed by Canada and the United States must first be for domestic and sanitary purposes, which relates to the health of people and recreation. The water then can be used for navigation, and last of all for power and irrigation. If power makes too great a demand on water it should be the duty of the International Joint Commission to inform the power people that they will have to curtail the use of water for
Supply-Transport
power to be made available for consumers. They should not be given all the power they want for any purpose, and should not be allowed to unnecessarily use water for power when there is a shortage. The use of power in this case should be restricted, just as it was during the war years.
While we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Transport I should like to draw another matter to the minister's attention. I refer to the despicable situation which exists at airports in Canada where monopoly franchises are granted to transportation companies to move passengers to and from these airports. I cannot see for the life of me how the Liberal party can agree to these monopoly franchises that are granted to transportation companies for the transportation of people to and from the centres of cities and airports, and I have in mind from Ottawa to Uplands, Montreal to Dorval and Toronto to Malton, and then claim great credit for all they are doing to keep down prices.
I have in my hand a press release issued by the Department of Transport on March 27. At that time the Minister of Transport did not have a doctorate from the University of Manitoba, and the press release refers to him only as Hon. J. W. Pickersgill. I want to congratulate him on his honorary degree of yesterday and, as a newspaperman and friend of Lord Thomson of Fleet, I should like to congratulate him on the honorary degree he received a few days ago from the Memorial University of St. John's, Newfoundland. I sincerely hope he does not consider the degree he received from the Memorial University any less appropriate than the one he received from Manitoba because the chancellor of Memorial University is not a Canadian citizen. He had to become a citizen of the United Kingdom because of the provisions of the Canadian Citizenship Act. Lord Thomson was born and raised in Canada and loves his country better than any other on earth.
Tomorrow the minister, who issued this press release, is going to receive a hood from the Abbot of Bishop's University. I wish to congratulate him again on this honour. When he comes back to the house next week no doubt he will be able to explain to us how the Liberal party can appear to be walking down both sides of the road at the same time, particularly in respect of transportation between the downtown centres and the Malton airport, the Uplands airport, the Dorval airport and between the Ottawa Union Station and downtown Ottawa.

May 26, 1967
Supply-Transport
This press release dated March 27, 1967, relates to the fact that Canadian Pacific Airlines has been granted permission to fly-more aircraft in Canada during Expo. In the middle of this press release from the Department of Transport at Ottawa the Minister of Transport issued the following statement regarding transcontinental air services in Canada. The second paragraph reads:
A well known British aviation consultant, Mr. Stephen Wheatcroft, who had been employed by the previous government to report on this matter, was asked to make a further report. His report received last year indicated that the service by C.P.A. on the domestic-transcontinental route Van-couver-Winnipeg-Montreal-Toronto, limited to a once daily round trip, while it had not shown any indication of producing either major improvements in efficiency or new traffic, had led to a wider public satisfaction as a result of the availability of choice between two carriers.
After the minister learned from Mr. Wheatcroft that there was wider public satisfaction as a result of availability of choice between two carriers, why would he not consider there would be wider public satisfaction as the result of availability of choice in getting to and from these airports such as Uplands, Malton and Dorval, to name only three? I believe the statement that there is wider public satisfaction as a result of availability of choice is a true and accurate statement, but why does the cabinet limit the choice at airports to a monopoly situation by granting these franchises?
I have in my hand the last report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on consumer credit, under the joint chairmanship of hon. Senator David Croll and Mr. Ron Basford. It is dated April 25, 1967, and is a progress report. At page 3470 under the paragraph heading "Consumer standards and consumer protection" we find the following statement:
It is essential for the government to take all measures within its power to foster the welfare of the consumer.
That is a nice broad statement. Who would disagree with it? The paragraph then continues as follows:
In particular, the government has a responsibility for protecting the consumer against all forms of exploitation.
Let me point out to you that the rates charged by the transportation people from airports to the centres of cities they serve are considerably higher than the rates charged by independent cab companies, and I can give you a specific example. When I use the authorized transportation service from Malton

to Toronto it costs me $4.50, or if they happen to go down Jane St. and get into another self-imposed zone it costs $4.75. If I call up the Northwest Taxi or a Yellow Cab the trip costs $3.50 or $3.75. There is a difference of one dollar in favour of the franchised carrier. The independent cab people are willing to provide this service at the lesser price, and the same situation applies in Montreal. I gave you the figures for Toronto because I have alternated between the two companies deliberately to have a comparison to present to the house, e (4:30 p.m.)
Continuing to quote from the report of the consumer credit committee, we read:
One aspect of this responsibility was referred by the government in July, 1966, to the Economic Council of Canada for investigation. The terms of reference of the study to be carried out are:
"In the light of the government's long term economic objectives to study and advise regarding: . .. (b) combines, mergers, monopolies and restraint of trade;"
If a monopoly position does not exist with regard to the airports in Canada when it comes to the transfer of passengers, I would like to know what else you can call it. And if it is not a restraint of trade, since other taxi companies are not allowed to stand at the airports and pick up passengers I do not know what the words "restraint of trade" mean. This situation is made even more ridiculous as far as the Liberal party is concerned when you read the debates in the House of Commons in 1951 at the time the amendment to the Combines Investigation Act was introduced to stop the maintenance of resale prices. I have been a businessman for 40 years and believe I look on things from a businessman's viewpoint. I did not agree with the Liberal government's attitude in 1951 when they brought in the amendment to the Combines Investigation Act in order to prevent the maintenance of resale prices at the retail level, and I do not agree with the act even at this time.
But listen to Hon. Lionel Chevrier, minister of transport in the St. Laurent government, speaking in this House of Commons on December 28, 1951. He is pointing out how the Liberal government is going to smash these maintained prices. Yes, sir; it takes the Liberal party to smash maintained prices, and it also takes the Liberal party to grant monopolies to these airport transportation companies. Mr. Chevrier said:
Hon. members will recall first of all that the royal commission on prices under the chairmanship of Professor Clifford Curtis of Queen's university
May 26, 1967

was-and I quote his remarks-"impressed by the degrea to which individual manufacturers fix the sale prices of their products, and so narrow the area in which price competition amongst wholesalers and retailers is operative."
There is very little competition among taxi companies when only one company is granted the right to run in and out of an airport. Mr. Chevrier continued:
That commission, which included a representative of the women of Canada, in the person of Mrs. Sutherland, and a prominent representative of the Quebec co-operative movement, Mr. Bois, recommended that the combines investigation commission give careful consideration and study to the problem, with a view to devising measures to deal with it.
Then, later on, we had the MacQuarrie committee, an impartial and distinguished group of Canadians who made a study of resale price maintenance and reached the unanimous recommendation that the practice is not in the public interest and should be made illegal. That was a unanimous recommendation, and there was no reservation to it whatever.
There has been criticism of that report on the ground that the committee did not obtain sufficient factual evidence. I am not much impressed by that kind of criticism. What I think is significant is that men like Mr. Justice MacQuarrie from Nova Scotia, and Mr. Curtis from British Columbia, Mr. Lamontagne from Quebec and Dr. Mackintosh from Queen's university, Kingston, Ontario, were satisfied that they had enough information to reach the unanimous conclusion that resale price maintenance is not in the public interest. I am quite sure that if they had felt that more information was required before reaching such a conclusion they would not have hesitated to say so.
That is Hon. Lionel Chevrier, then minister of transport, speaking in this house in 1951. What better way is there to maintain the price than to have a monopoly position so that the rates you set are not open to competition by anyone.
I came into Ottawa on Monday by the evening train from Toronto. I could not get airplane reservations for Tuesday, so came down on the evening train. I was interested in the fact that when this train, with a tremendous group of holiday people returning to Ottawa from Toronto, Belleville, Kingston, Port Hope and other places along the line, got to Ottawa station, passengers were jumping into Arrow cabs, Capital cabs, Diamond cabs and Buske cabs. I wrote the names of the taxi companies down. The franchise is with Blue Line, but the passengers from the train were jumping into the taxis of these other companies. I stood at the doorway for a while watching the service that Blue Line is supposed to give under the monopoly position which it holds. It was quite evident that Blue Line could not handle this traffic and they
Supply-Transport
were allowing these other companies to pick up whatever traffic they could.
I telephoned some of these private companies during the week and asked whether they had to kick in anything to Blue Line because they were picking up these passengers on Monday night. Blue Line could not convey the volume of traffic offered. They told me they did not make any kick-back to Blue Line, and when Blue Line are flooded with business they do not object to these other taxi companies servicing the people at the station. If Blue Line do not object to other taxi companies servicing people at the station on a holiday night, why should they object to them picking up passengers on any other night of the year?
We live in a competitive age. I have lived with competition in the business world, and I can tell you that it does not do any harm. It keeps you sharp, I can assure you. Why should a monopoly position be allowed to develop in Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa or anywhere else? The situation in Ottawa is pinpointed in this respect. There is a new hotel opening here, the Skyline. One taxi company has a monopoly position to run from the station to the Chateau Laurier and the Lord Elgin, and another company in the city of Ottawa wishes to make a similar arrangement in respect of the new Skyline hotel, running out to the Ottawa station at $1 a passenger. They will even make a second stop at West-gate shopping centre. They are trying to get the government to give them the right to pick up passengers at the station and run them to the Skyline hotel and the Westgate shopping centre. I wonder what reaction this will have? According to the report of the consumer credit committee and Mr. Chevrier, the Liberal party is in favour of competition in order to keep prices down. It will be interesting to see whether a second franchise is granted at the Ottawa railway station to a taxi firm so they can operate to the Skyline hotel. I wonder whether they will be allowed to compete for business at the airport and at the station, as they should be allowed to do.
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

Does the hon. member realize that the Skyline hotel is approximately three quarters of a mile beyond the Chateau, and the price of a taxi is 25 cents less than from the railway station to the Chateau?

May 25, 1967
Supply-Transport

I am glad to have that contribution to the debate. I am pointing out that the federal cabinet claims that it wants to keep a competitive position in business in this country, but business is being prevented from competing by a cabinet which accepts the report of the consumer credit committee and has enacted measures to prevent resale price maintenance, but on the other hand grants monopoly positions to people who are thus able to maintain any price they want to maintain.
With regard to Malton, I point out that I was told once the reason the contract was not thrown open to public competition was that the original contract was less than $5,000. It is quite interesting to know that the original contract was less than $5,000, because within three years a 51 per cent interest in the company was sold to the present owner for better than $1 million. How you can expect the public to believe the statement that the original contract was entered into without public tender because it was less than $5,000, yet within three or four years the controlling interest in the company was sold for over $1 million to a group of bus lines in western Ontario, is beyond my comprehension. But the public are supposed to buy that and are not supposed to protest too much about it.
I had intended to speak on the question of land fill in lake Ontario, which is still going on despite the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I do not know of anything authoritative on the matter, but I have seen a letter to the effect that the Navigable Waters Protection Act is now under the authority of the Minister of Transport rather than under the authority of the Minister of Public Works. However, in the Navigable Waters Protection Act it is stated definitely in the interpretation clause that "minister" means the Minister of Public Works. I would like to discuss the question of illegal land fill in lake Ontario, but I understand the discussion continues next week with the Minister of Transport and perhaps I could deal with it then. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would simply like to ask the minister whether the Department of Transport is still making informal references to the Board of Broadcast Governors on all cable community antenna television applications.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The regulations are that the Department of Transport shall rule on these applications, and the cable companies want the department to rule on them. Are they now being referred

to the Board of Broadcast Governors informally?

I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit me to say one word. It is my intention on Monday-I reached this conclusion because of what was said by the hon. members for Vancouver East and Quadra earlier today, and I felt it would help them to answer some of the questions they raised about the development of Vancouver harbour-to ask the port manager in Vancouver to release publicly a report on the Vancouver harbour traffic trends and facility analysis which was done by the British Columbia Research Council. I have had this report for a few days but only had time to read on the way back from Winnipeg yesterday where I received an honorary degree, which contributed materially to my understanding of the report. The report itself is very interesting and illuminating. It is done by a very reputable body indeed, as the hon. gentleman would recognize.
I think it will contribute very materially to an understanding of the problems and of what is being done to meet them, in what is already the second largest port in Canada and on the Pacific coast of North America. I think, of our largest ports, it is the most rapidly growing one. I intend to make copies available to all hon. members from the metropolitan area of Vancouver some time on Monday.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to take advantage of the suggestion made by the minister today to hear opinions and suggestions from all hon. members of the house with regard to his department. I would just like to raise briefly one particular problem which has to do with the discrimination against northern Ontario by Air Canada. I want to make it perfectly clear from the start that when I speak of this discrimination I am not referring to the staff of Air Canada. I would like to take this occasion to pay the highest possible tribute to the Air Canada staff. I include not only the hostesses and the operators of the airplanes but also the staff in the various airports across the country who have demonstrated nothing but the greatest patience and courtesy and have given a very high standard of service.
The matter I am raising is not new. I have raised it before with the minister and his officials as well as with his predecessor, now
May 26, 1967



the Minister of Public Works. In fact, this complaint goes back to the days when Hon. Leon Balcer was minister of transport. This matter is particularly highlighted this year, and becomes even more a responsibility of the government, owing to the fact that this government has spent millions and millions of dollars to attract people to the wonderful show at Expo.
Of course, in order to get to Expo we have to consider the means of getting there. It is a very interesting point that Air Canada fares average in the neighbourhood of six cents a mile. Passengers travelling from Timmins to Toronto pay approximately that rate, and passengers travelling from Toronto to Ottawa also pay that rate. However, if one wants to travel from Ottawa to Timmins one has to pay $19 for the first 12 miles, or to get 12 miles closer to one's destination. I have raised this matter with the president of Air Canada, with whom I have exchanged considerable correspondence over the years, and as I have said, I have raised it with various ministers. If the ministers of transport of this country can be resistant, I would like to let them know that I can be just as persistent as they can be resistant. I intend to keep raising this matter until something is done to correct it. The distance from Timmins to Toronto is approximately 453 miles by highway. The return air fare over that distance costs $54, which is approximately six cents a mile. This is certainly a very competitive rate. I do not think one can travel that distance by car for that cost.
The distance between Timmins and Ottawa is about 12 miles further, or about 465 miles in all, but the difference in the return fare is $92 as compared to $54. Thus, it costs $1.50 a mile to travel the first 12 miles from Ottawa to Timmins. I do not deny the right of Air Canada to route passengers travelling from Timmins to Ottawa and Montreal around by Toronto if they wish to do so, but I do think it is very unfair to charge passengers for that distance. As is well known, we have in the north country a great number of French Canadian people. Many of them would like to make the trip to Expo this year, but they are met with what I can only describe as a discriminatory rate.
I should also like to say that it is interesting to note the transport policy adopted by this government. As I mentioned before, the air service between Timmins and Toronto is excellent. The train service from that area to Ottawa and Montreal is extremely bad, and so is the air service. I do not know why it is 27053-41
Supply-Transport
that when the train service is good we have a good air service as well but when the train service is bad, we supply poor air service. The president of Air Canada has given all kinds of excuses for this, none of which I can accept as valid. I was told by Air Canada first of all that they tried this sort of flight about ten years ago when the Timmins airport first opened, but they found there was an insufficient number of passengers to warrant the flight. Anybody with any realization of the situation today knows that far more people travel by air than was the case ten years ago. The train service which I mentioned has deteriorated in the same period of time. When I was first elected to the house some ten years ago, if one wanted to travel to Ottawa by train one could get a berth right in Timmins. A year or two later one had to go down to Porquis Junction, a year or two later one had to go to Englehart, and a year or two later one had to go to North Bay to get a berth. Now, one has to change trains about two o'clock in the morning and continue the rest of the trip to Ottawa and Montreal on a train which has neither berth or diner. The only other way one can get train service is to drive some 70 miles over what I believe is the only highway in Canada that is in worse condition than the trans-Canada highway as it goes across Ontario. Then, you catch the only convenient evening train which is the same train one would normally catch from North Bay. This is the train which has neither diner service nor berth, and is certainly a very uncomfortable mode of transportation.
I was also informed by the president of Air Canada, and I have the correspondence in my files, that Air Canada has made a check of the number of passengers travelling from the Timmins area to Ottawa and Montreal over a certain period of time. As a result, the company has concluded that the number of passengers does not warrant a direct flight between those points. How can a passenger service be built up if one has to pay six cents a mile to go to Toronto but the cost is almost twice as much for the additional 12 miles distance between Toronto and Ottawa? Of course this situation applies also to the passengers travelling from Montreal.
One other point which emphasizes the need for some corrective action in this field was illustrated to me the other day when I had lunch with a former member of this house, Mr. Jake Schultz from Winnipeg. He had been out to the west coast this year and he drove down this way. He said that the trans-Canada highway all the way across Canada

May 26, 1967
Supply-Transport
up to the Ontario border is in excellent condition. However, he said that once he crossed the Ontario border and travelled through northern Ontario the road was in such bad condition it was dangerous to life and limb.
I realize that this is not the particular responsibility of the minister but is primarily the responsibility of the government of Ontario. Even so, this matter would be under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works rather than the Minister of Transport. However, I made this point in order to direct the attention of the minister to the additional need for some corrective measure to be taken, particularly this year in view of the fact that everybody is drawn to Expo in Montreal. We certainly want to make the travelling facilities attractive to the Canadian people who will visit Expo so as to warrant the expenditure on advertising. So, I would urge the minister to use his influence to try to do one of two things, either establish a direct flight from Timmins-North Bay-Ottawa-Montreal or, if this is not practicable, then at least establish a flight with fares which would be equitable as compared to other flights across this country.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, it has been a while since I made any remarks concerning transport, but there has not been the sort of improvement which I had hoped to see in air services. I am reminded of the years when the Conservative government first allowed C.P.A. to have some air transport rights in Canada. As I recall the arguments advanced at that time by trans-Canada air lines, as it was called then, as well as by some hon. members on the other side of the house, there was a feeling that since we had a national air line it was necessary that it be put in a position where it could start to pay its way as soon as possible. A fear was expressed that there was not enough business to afford competition. They said that we were putting Air Canada in a position where it was likely to continue at a deficit or would not be able to afford to buy new planes so as to provide the kind of service we wanted it to give. As I recall, the president of Air Canada at that time, Mr. McGregor, in his arguments before the transport committee, said that the plans were for T.C.A. to acquire new aeroplanes to take care of the increase in the business. However, the cost of these new aeroplanes was such that they had to have that increase in business that was anticipated in order to

be able to provide a service and to have a chance of breaking even.
The argument was then put forward that the other carrier, the C.P.A., would be glad to compete just for the increase in air traffic. In other words, once we had obtained a sufficient level of business for the national airline to be able to meet expenses, the increase in traffic should be thrown open to competition. They felt that in this way Air Canada would be assured of a situation in which they could break even, and that we would then be giving service to the country by having two airlines competing for the increase in traffic. It is my contention that we made the right move by allowing C.P.A. some rights in domestic airlines but that we have not gone nearly far enough. It is obvious to anyone who does any amount of travelling that the increase in air traffic was grossly underestimated by trans-Canada air lines and by the government. I am sure that the increase in air traffic today is such that had it been foreseen, we would have had much less objection to T.C.A.'s arguments regarding what competition would do to them. I am sure we would have had much more enthusiasm even from C.P.A., and a stronger bargaining position in order to get more service.
The situation in western Canada today is such that, even without Expo, we are not getting the service to which we are entitled. Businessmen as well as tourists must line up for a long time in order to get reservations. When we have Expo, which puts an extra load on the lines, something has to give. I know that in the city of Edmonton representations have been made for some time for another air carrier. He said: Mr. Speaker, centennial year is, I believe, an appropriate time to discuss and to assess the meaning and the significance of Canadian citizenship. To me it is a matter of gratification that the first private member's bill to be discussed at this centennial session of parliament is this bill, which is designed and introduced by me to serve a threefold purpose, each of the purposes being related to Canadian citizenship. For in this very special year, sir, the year of Canada's centennial, nothing could be more significant or vital than our dedication to a common Canadian nationality.
The basic purpose of confederation was to create a new nationality, one which, as Professor Frank H. Underhill has so well stated, would include but transcend-and I heavily underline the word "transcend"-the two main groups of English speaking and French speaking Canadians. To those two groups, divided in race, language and religion but united at confederation in a new nationality, has been joined the representatives of many other people-a genuine third force in our nation.
Now, sir, why do I describe the basic purpose of confederation as the creation of a new nationality? Permit me to read the words of the second paragraph of the first speech from the throne ever delivered in this parliament on November 7, 1867:
I congratulate you on the Legislative sanction which has been given by the Imperial Parliament to the Act of Union, under the provisions of which we are now assembled and which has laid the foundations of a new nationality, that I trust and believe will, ere long, extend its bounds from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean.
The words "the foundation of a new nationality" were uttered by Lord Monck, Canada's first Governor General, but most probably their author was Sir John A. Macdonald. Certainly those words were approved by the first cabinet, which included many of the fathers of confederation, the architects of the new nationality, men of French heritage, men of English, Scots and Irish heritage. What they proclaimed-and again I underline this-was the foundation of a new nationality, neither French, English, Scots, Irish, Welsh nor that of any other "old land", but one

DEBATES	May 26, 1967
which was to be unique as well as new and which was to bear the proud name "Canadian". It was not to be two nationalities, Mr. Speaker, nor three, nor four-just one.
This view of the intentions of the fathers of confederation was stated by Professor Frank
H.	Underhill with his usual clarity in the Massey Lectures, published under the title "The Image of Confederation". I should like to refer to an extract from page 1 of those lectures:
The experiment of the new nationality that they thus proclaimed was of a nationality that should link together a variety of rather isolated, little colonial communities scattered across the northern half of the continent, and that, in particular, should include and transcend the two groups of English speaking and French speaking Canadians, divided though they were in race, language, and religion. That is, it was a complex nationality; and they were well aware of their own boldness in the initiation of this experiment.
A nation is a body of men who have done great things together in the past and who hope to do great things together in the future. What makes them into a nation is not necessarily community of race, language, and religion, though these are powerful forces when they are present; it is their common history and traditions, their experience of living together, their having done great things together in the past, and their determination to continue doing great things together in the future.
I should like to repeat the words "their determination to continue doing great things together in the future", because I think that that is the real spirit of this nation of Canada.
In that light, Mr. Speaker, and with that background I would ask the house to give favourable consideration to this bill which would revise the Canadian Citizenship Act in three particulars.
The first problem dealt with by this bill is that of children born abroad to Canadian citizens. Under the law as it now stands a child born outside Canada of a member of Canada's armed forces or a member of the diplomatic or other public service or, indeed, of any other Canadian will lose his Canadian citizenship unless two separate things are done-and these things must be done about 20 years apart. First, the fact of his birth must be registered at a Canadian office abroad within two years of its occurrence.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Second, the individual born abroad must file between the ages of 21 or 24 a declaration of retention of Canadian citizenship. Today there are large numbers of Canadians serving or engaged outside of Canada; undoubtedly the number will grow. Many of the children of these Canadians born outside Canada are
May 26, 1967	COMMONS
likely to lose their Canadian citizenship, and lose it unwittingly, either through the failure of their parents to register the births abroad or through their own failure between the ages of 21 or 24 to file a declaration of retention.
True, he who loses his citizenship for either reason may regain it, but to do so he must file a petition for resumption of Canadian citizenship; the minister has a discretion in the granting of that petition. In my submission that is to make second class citizens of those children who are born abroad to Canadian citizens. To place the children of Canadian citizens who are serving their country abroad in the armed forces or in some other form of public service, as missionaries or as members of the Company of Young Canadians, in a category different from the children of Canadians performing the same duties in Canada is discriminatory and, I submit, a genuine hardship to the parents and children.
Now, you sir, as a distinguished member of the bar-and I proclaim that the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) who is now the Acting Speaker is a distinguished member of the bar, as is the usual incumbent of the Speaker's chair, you will know that under the old rule of nationality, which was related to the status on British subjects, dual registration was required only in the instance of the child, born abroad, the father of whom was also born abroad. In other words, the second generation born outside the realm needed to act to preserve its status. The rule, I think, made more sense than our existing rule under the present Canadian Citizenship Act.
This bill, sir, would preserve without registration or declaration the status of natural born citizen to any child born outside Canada to a Canadian citizen who was enlisted in the armed forces of Canada or was a public servant of the dominion or any provincial government, or was employed outside Canada by any firm, business, company or organization-religious or otherwise-the principal office of which was in Canada, or who was employed by an international organization in which Canada participates. This would cover virtually all the births abroad. For persons not within these categories the existing provisions of registration of birth and declaration of intention would continue to apply.
My submission this afternoon to the house is that we ought not to leave the children born abroad to our armed forces, to our diplomats, to our foreign aid officers, to our missionaries-to use only a few examples-in
DEBATES	641
Canadian Citizenship Act the existing state of "nationality no man's land".
Sir, since the bill was introduced I have had many calls from persons in the armed forces and from officers in the Department of External Affairs expressing their resentment at the secondary status of their children -children which have been born abroad. One officer indicated that of his four children the first and third had been born in Canada when he was on duty in this country but that the second and fourth were born in different countries while he was on overseas duty. These brothers and sisters have a different status as Canadian citizens-an anomaly surely within one family.
Mr. Speaker, the second proposed amendment arises out of frustrations I experienced as minister of citizenship and immigration in being unable to deal with applications for citizenship which were rejected, and which I was not able to deal With, for a two year period from the date of such rejection. Let me illustrate, and I think the matter will become clear.
In one instance I satisfied myself that the rejection was made on grounds which arose from mistaken identity. Had the applicant been guilty of the conduct alleged, the grounds for rejection would have been valid; it was not the applicant however, but another, of similar name, who had been guilty. Yet the minister was deprived by statute of doing justice for a two year period. I say that that situation is intolerable-although the likelihood of the situation arising again will be minimized by the proposed creation of a court of citizenship appeal. I emphasize that the court of citizenship appeal proposed in the government measure has nothing to do with the minister's final discretionary authority, and particularly where such authority is related to security matters. Nevertheless the minister, I believe, should have the right in special cases to deal with rejected application before the expiry of the two years, and that is what this bill proposes.
Finally, sir, this bill seeks to give full and absolute equality of status to all Canadian citizens, irrespective of whether they are natural born or naturalized. At present, for a number of reasons, Canadian citizens who are not natural born may be deprived of citizenship, whereas natural born citizens may not be so deprived for identical reasons. I say that this is a serious and regrettable discrimination which is resented deeply by naturalized Canadians. When the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), the
May 26, 1967

Canadian Citizenship Act present hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate, was in opposition, he railed against this and in 1959 he introduced a private member's bill on the subject. Four successive speeches from the throne promised to rectify it, and the hon. gentleman for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) has talked of it on a number of occasions. Bill No. S-59 of the last session and Bill No. S-4 of this session-now on the Order Paper-deal with this matter, and Bill No. S-4 purports to do something about it. The bill I now discuss, sir, was first drafted before the original Bill No. S-59 was first introduced in the Senate.
This bill would make it clear that hereafter, under no circumstances, could a Canadian citizen who is not natural born lose his citizenship for any cause which would not in the same circumstances lead to the loss of Canadian citizenship by a natural born citizen. I believe that this is to be prefered to the retention of the power of revocation where citizenship was obtained "by concealment of material circumstances"-a vague and dangerous term-as proposed in Bill No. S-4. That is a government bill, and we shall discuss that on another occasion.
This bill now moved, Mr. Speaker, has three purposes and I hope that all three purposes will commend themselves to the house and to members on all sides.

There is nothing political, there is nothing partisan in this bill. I believe it could very well be accepted by the government and accepted by the house. By the grapevine, I hear that the government proposes to refer its bill which is on the order paper, Bill S-4, to the standing committee on Indian Affairs, human rights and citizenship and immigration. What would be most agreeable to me is that if this bill, after being debated until five minutes to six o'clock, could then be referred to that committee and given the opportunity for detailed study which I venture to suggest it genuinely deserves.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief because I believe in trying to promote the concept that bills introduced by private members should be sent to a committee, regardless of their place of origin in the house, in order that a committee, and consequently government, may be able to draw upon all the brains in the house and not only on those which happen to reside in the heads of cabinet ministers. Of course, if those appeals had been listened to during the time the hon. gentleman was in the cabinet of the Conservative government, we might not now have to make such appeals because there would be an automatic procedure to refer public bills in the hands of private members to committee. Thus, we would have advanced a little more than we have into the field of reform of parliament.
After listening to the very effusive and perhaps voluble remarks of the hon. member for Carleton, I rather expected a glistening and shining document to be presented to the house, and perhaps the bill in so far as it goes falls within that category. But I think even the hon. member would admit it does have, not deficiencies, but that there are some items relating to matters of citizenship in Canada that could be included in it. In other words, the bill is not completely exhaustive of the necessity of altering our citizenship act to comply with the sense of what has been advocated by the hon. member for Carleton in his speech, and what has been advocated by others over the years.
I am not going to try to transgress on the rules of the house by commenting on Bill S-4, which also deals with the citizenship act, but it would seem to me to be an admirable course to take, to remove the present requirement that a person be of landed immigrant status for five years before he can make application for citizenship.
I have advocated this on other occasions, and I reiterate it now. If this bill does go to a committee, and if the government takes the course of referring Bill S-4 to a committee as well, the committee might well consider reducing the present five year requirement to

one year. Not only do I think the five years inordinately long, but also within it there is an element of discrimination because, as I understand the law, it says that if a woman becomes the wife of a Canadian citizen she can apply for citizenship after one year. That is why I choose the one year period and advocate making it applicable to everyone. The one year period is now contained in the law, but it applies only to a woman who becomes the wife of a Canadian citizen.
Conversely if a man becomes the husband of a Canadian citizen-and this is the discriminatory part-he has to wait for five years before he can make an application for citizenship. It would seem to me that at least the justice of equality, of making men equal with women before the law, should find its way into the Citizenship Act.
I presume we have to have some period specified and I suggest this one year period. I suggest we should make it universally applicable to anyone who comes to Canada from Europe, Asia, Africa, any country large or small. I suggest we should base our requirements for citizenship not upon the rituals that exist now, of having people learn by rote the names of the Great Lakes, the names of the highest mountains, how many provinces there are, and who happens to form the government for the time being, but rather place a greater emphasis on the intentions and the hopes that the individual has, on his concepts of Canada, his concepts of citizenship and of responsibility to mankind and to society.
If we placed more emphasis upon this, and less upon learning from a text prepared by the department itself about what one should say when one goes before a citizenship court,
I think we would be starting off on developing a far greater understanding and appreciation of what Canada is.

Within the amendment as presented by this Bill C-2 I wonder why, for example, the only children born out of wedlock who automatically would be Canadian citizens would be those in cases where it was the mother who served outside of Canada. When one starts discussing children born out of wedlock in cases where the father is serving outside of Canada, I know difficulties in determining paternity arise. It does seem to me, however, that this has been one of the most distressing aspects of the situations in wartime or peacetime, where large bodies of armed forces have been outside the country and where in several countries of the world a sizeable proportion of second class citizens have been left behind when the armed forces have withdrawn.
844	COMMONS
Canadian Citizenship Act
These are citizens who have no claim to the citizenship of the countries to which their fathers belong and who have not been received by the country in which the armed forces were serving. A moral problem, and one which admittedly is perhaps unsolvable, has remained through the years in such countries. I have nothing but praise for the subsequent clauses of the bill and particularly the part of the bill which would remove any second class status from naturalized citizens. Having been a teacher of social studies, I had the embarrassing experience of a bright student asking me why some Canadian citizens were second class citizens lacking the full rights of citizenship even though citizenship had been granted to them because what had been granted to them was not as complete as the citizenship of the native born. When that question was asked, I was placed in the embarrassing position of having no defence whatsoever to make for this most irrational, illogical and discriminatory situation.
I felt that surely, if citizenship is to be granted at all, it should be granted completely. Therefore, I would approve wholeheartedly of this bill. If it should be referred to the committee, I would hope that the committee and subsequently this house would move as rapidly as possible to implement the amendment to the act which would make Canadian citizenship a factor that is indivisible so that it would have the same full meaning and value for anyone who held it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE DISCRIMINATION AGAINST CHILDREN BORN ABROAD, REJECTED APPLICANTS ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to sincerely congratulate the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) for his moving speech this afternoon and especially for his introductory remarks.
At the outset I must say that some of the points raised in this Bill C-2 are very well made. In fact, some of the proposals made by the hon. member for Carleton are included in Bill S-4 which was passed in the other place on May 10 and which was introduced here and given first reading on May 15.
Clauses 4 and 5 of Bill S-4 are almost identical to clauses 3 and 4 of this bill. The purpose is to remove the areas of discrimination which appear to exist between the natural born and the non-natural born Canadian. However, I think it is appropriate to retain the power to revoke citizenship which is obtained fraudulently and for this reason I do not agree that section 19(1) of the Canadian Citizenship Act should be repealed in its entirety. I do not consider that discrimination

DEBATES	May 26, 1967
can be charged by permitting revocation of citizenship obtained by false representation, fraud or concealment of material circumstances even though only the non-natural born Canadian can become a citizen by such malfeasance.
I am rather surprised that the hon. member for Carleton, who was a former minister of the crown then responsible for the administration of the Canadian Citizenship Act, would suggest that the minister be given discretion to shorten the two year delay period before which rejected applicants again have the right to re-apply for citizenship. I am sure that he is personally aware of the heavy responsibility carried by a minister when under the law he rejects an applicant for Canadian citizenship who has already satisfied a citizenship court that he is a fit and proper person worthy to receive the high honour of Canadian citizenship. It seems to me that such a decision is only reached after the most careful consideration of all the available information, and then applicants are only rejected in the national interest when there appears to be no other alternative.
In so far as applicants who are rejected by the courts are concerned, hon. members are aware that the citizenship act does not provide the minister with any discretion unless the court decision is favourable. To provide the minister with authority to direct a court to receive a new application would serve little or no purpose since the court could reject the new application on the same grounds as the previous rejection. However, I think the establishment of a citizenship appeal court, as proposed in clause 7 of Bill S-4, will achieve the real aim of the proposal found in clause 2 of this bill. Although it does not entitle a rejected applicant to file a new application before two years, such an applicant will be able to have his existing application reviewed by a higher court. This will protect his rights, particularly in cases where applicants consider that their qualifications have been unfairly assessed by the lower court or in cases such as have happened in the past where the rejection of an applicant appears to be contrary to the basic principle of freedom of religious belief or for that matter, disbelief which we profess as a basic right in Canada.

I now come to what I consider is the principal proposal in Bill C-2 which is found in the first clause. The explanatory note in the bill alleges that the registration
May 26, 1967	COMMONS
process required under the Canadian Citizenship Act for children of Canadians born abroad since January 1, 1947, is discriminatory particularly when related to the children of Canadians who are serving their country abroad either in the armed forces, the federal or provincial public services. This applies as well to Canadians in the private sector who are employed abroad by industry which is established in Canada and also to persons employed outside Canada by international agencies in which we participate.
I must admit that at first glance there seemed to be an element of discrimination in the existing law, particularly when related to children of Canadians serving abroad in the direct service of their country.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
On the other hand, I wondered if it would not be equally discriminatory to single out certain groups of Canadians by professions or occupations and give them what might be considered advantages over all other Canadians. As a result, I decided to do some research into the reason for this registration of birth abroad requirement to see whether it should be retained for all Canadians or deleted from the law completely.
I find that at page 506 of Hansard of April 2, 1946, the present minister of external affairs (Mr. Martin) who was then secretary of state, had this to say when comparing the requirements for Canadians born abroad after the new citizenship act came into effect with the provision then found in the Naturalization Act:
The principal difference is his. that in future all Canadian children born abroad will have to be registered within two years either at a diplomatic, consular or trade commissioner's office or in Ottawa. Hitherto registrations have not been necessary in all cases of children born abroad who have acquired the status provided for in existing legislation. There is, I believe, good reason for this. There is a slightly greater strictness in the new bill. Hereafter Canadian children born abroad will, as Canadians, have the right to entry into Canada. They have never had it before. In giving this important right it is felt necessary to have some record and some form of evidence that will serve for immigration purposes. Children born in Canada will in all cases have birth certificates. In a parallel manner we are requiring the registration of children born abroad, in order that there may be a basic record to establish their rights as Canadian citizens.
On reflection I have come to the conclusion that the registration requirement is both a good and a necessary provision even though some may say "merely more paper work". I don't think we would be helping those
DEBATES	645
Canadian Citizenship Act Canadians serving their country abroad by exempting them from this requirement.
I should like to point out to hon. members that government staff who are sent abroad, including forces personnel, are well briefed on the requirements of Canadian legislation which might affect them while outside Canada. To this end they are warned by their respective departments of the registration requirement related to children born abroad. It is the duty and responsibility of Canadian consular officials abroad to warn all Canadians of the requirements and, surely, it is not too much to expect them to personally remember to register their own children.
At any rate, once the birth is registered, there is a permanent basic record from which claims to citizenship can be confirmed. Departmental officials inform me that one of the greatest problems they face relates to the documentation required when a Canadian who was born outside this country 50 or 60 years ago suddenly finds himself in need of proof of his claim to being a Canadian by descent. He must document his parents' marriage, he must prove the father-child relationship and, in addition, he frequently must establish his own lawful admission to Canada for permanent residence. I am sure many hon. members have received letters from irate constituents complaining bitterly about the almost impossible task demanded of them by the citizenship officials to document their claim to the truth of the simple statement "I am a Canadian". Nevertheless, if Canadian citizenship is to retain its high value all this is necessary because proof of citizenship cannot be issued on the mere say so of every individual who claims to be a Canadian, but who was not born here.
On the other hand, let us look at the case of a 20 year old alleged Canadian who arrives at our border for the first time in this, our centennial year, and demands his right to come into Canada to attend the centennial ceremonies of "his country" but who has not equipped himself beforehand with proper travel documents and identification papers which will bear out his claim to being a Canadian. The fact is that if his birth was not registered he is not a Canadian. However, if his parents attended to the matter of registering his birth as required by the law since 1947, then a simple phone call or telegram to the citizenship authorities will confirm his claim to citizenship because it is a matter of record.
I know there are those who might say that this is all very well, but let the registration be
May 26. 1967

Canadian Citizenship Act merely an administrative process for establishing a basic record. However, the status itself should be automatically conferred at birth without the paper formality. How many of us would attend to this sort of detail if it were not absolutely essential? Many would be inclined to delay and procrastinate, and in the final analysis, no application for registration would be completed until an urgent need for proof of citizenship arose. Of course, it is this undesirable situation which should be avoided.
I should also mention that all Canadian passports carry a warning that children born abroad must be registered, and a further warning concerning the possibility of automatic loss of citizenship at age 24 if such Canadians are then domiciled abroad and have failed to exercise their right to protect their Canadian citizenship.
Here again this bill alleges discrimination against children born abroad of parents in certain professions or occupations who were required to live outside Canada. This is because such a person may inadvertently fail to take the necessary steps under the act to file a declaration of retention between his 21st and 24th birthdays. Of course, if he has never come to Canada or having come here has moved away again, he will automatically lose his birthright on his 24th birthday.
Earlier I said that at first glance I was inclined to agree that the existing provision seems to provide a discriminatory element against children of Canadians serving their country abroad. As I pointed out, the registration requirement provides a control measure related to citizenship by descent and ensures that such Canadians are citizens of record just as their brother and sister Canadians born in Canada are recorded under the provincial birth registration requirements.
In essence, we have here a further control measure which seems to be related to the fact there is an outward movement of Canadians to other countries, particularly to our great and friendly neighbour to the south. By this provision, children born outside Canada of such migrating Canadians lose their citizenship at age 24, but have the right to protect their nationality by filing a declaration of retention. This right is usually only exercised by those families who maintain strong ties and associations with their country of origin. I am rather inclined to the view that the birth registration requirement is sufficient


control. It is unlikely that successive generations of Canadians would carry out the registration procedure unless strong Canadian connections had been maintained.
In the latter instance, no doubt they would make very desirable Canadian citizens and little or no harm could result if a family of Canadian origin acted in accordance with the law and exercised their legal right to register children through a number of future generations.
Having said all this, it seems to me that the experts should be asked to consider this point in relation to possible future changes in the act. It seems to me that consideration might be given to dropping this provision as it relates to all Canadians born abroad or, conversely, substantial reasons should be advanced for its retention without any exceptions. I should mention, however, that as the law now stands, any Canadian who has lost his status under this provision may be permitted to resume it.
It is for these reasons that I consider it would be more appropriate at this time to approve Bill S-4 which has already received first reading, and leave consideration of other changes including those referred to in the bill introduced by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) until the entire law is under revision.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a particular pleasure to take part in this debate on the first private member's bill in our centennial session, particularly because of my strong interest in the subject of Canadian citizenship and, parenthetically, because I have the opportunity of supporting a bill put forward by my own member of parliament for the time being, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell).

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE DISCRIMINATION AGAINST CHILDREN BORN ABROAD, REJECTED APPLICANTS ETC.
speechtext:
I hope to be here for some years, but perhaps the member for Carleton will be different after the next election. The bill of the hon. member reflects the concern of many Canadians that there is a kind of second-class citizenship inherent in our Canadian Citizenship Act. Many of us on both sides of the house have for some time been putting forward suggestions for the removal of this discrimination. I am pleased to see that some of our representations are bearing fruit in the government bill which will reach us as S-4.
May 26, 1987
When that bill is under discussion in the house and in committee I presume the hon. member for Carleton will want to make suggestions for amendments, and I think that would be an ideal time to consider the ideas which are included in his private member's bill. I am also concerned about discrimination in another direction against our new citizens. I am concerned about the discrimination, that appears to be inherent in our laws, to which immigrants are exposed before they have the opportunity of becoming Canadian citizens.
I look back to the debate on the introduction of the Canadian Citizenship Act in 1946 and see that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), then secretary of state, moved second reading of the bill he said, as reported at page 504, volume I of Hansard for the session of 1946:
One thing we hope to do, following the passage of this measure, is to provide a more effective and impressive ceremony of admission into the Canadian family. Our citizenship is made up not only of people born in this country and of people who acquired domicile as British subjects under the Immigration Act, but of many thousands of new Canadians living in all parts of our country who have come from other lands and who have made a notable contribution to the development of Canada. There are people who came from many parts of central Europe and who are now living and working as Canadians on our farms and in our factories. Many of those people came here without being able to speak the two languages of the country and without being accustomed to its traditions. Most of them have rendered notable service to Canada. We should not lose the opportunity of impressing ourselves and reminding them that just as we are glad to welcome them to our shores, now that they are here they should enjoy with us the full measure of partnership in the Canadian community.
Under our present laws those who come to us from shores other than those of the British commonwealth do not enjoy a full measure of partnership in the Canadian community. I certainly would not deprecate the connection and the very warm affection that exists between Canadians and the mother country of so many of us and so many of our ancestors, the United Kingdom. But I suggest that we should consider very carefully whether the time has now passed, in this centennial year, when we can afford to put more stress on origin than we do on citizenship.
Canadian Citizenship Act
We And that under our electoral laws immigrants from countries other than those of the commonwealth are discriminated against. In order to vote at a federal election a person must be 21 years of age or over, a Canadian citizen or other British subject. In the case of a British subject he must be a person who resided in Canada for 12 months immediately preceding polling day.
The argument is put forward very often that naturally a person coming from a British country, with British parliamentary traditions, is more familiar with our democratic processes and our history and therefore should have rights superior to those afforded immigrants from other countries. But I would suggest that there is no longer any logic to this argument. There have been so many changes in our commonwealth that a great many commonwealth countries do not accord Canadians the same voting rights and rights of candidacy in their countries as we accord them here. In fact, we accord these rights to citizens of countries which are no longer in the commonwealth or which do not consider themselves to be within the commonwealth. We accord these rights to citizens of the Republic of Ireland. We accord these rights to citizens of the Republic of South Africa. We accord these rights to British subjects who are residents of Rhodesia but apparently do not now consider themselves to be members of our commonwealth.
Mr. Speaker, I think the least we could do in amending the citizenship act is recognize this kind of discrimination, ensuring for instance that the stress placed upon a person being a British subject does not accentuate the discrimination against others which is already inherent in our laws. I hope that the suggestions of my member of parliament will be considered very carefully when Bill No. S-4 is before the house. I am sure that the minister and her officials will consider his suggestions very carefully between now and that time.
